intro: Between 1914 and 1945, Americans lived through two world wars, a wild decade of boom and change, and the worst economic crisis in the nation's history. A child born in 1910 could have seen soldiers sail to France, watched cars and radios fill American homes, stood in a Depression bread line and then worked in a war factory or fought overseas, all before turning 35.

These crises changed what Americans expected from their government. After World War I, many wanted the nation to stay out of the world's troubles. The Great Depression led millions to believe that the national government should help people in hard times. World War II pulled the United States into the center of world affairs, where it has remained ever since.

In every crisis, Americans argued about freedom and fairness. Who could speak freely in wartime? Who could immigrate? Who got help and who was left out? African Americans, women, immigrants, Mexican Americans, Native Americans and Japanese Americans all fought for their place in the nation, sometimes while serving it in war.
bigQuestion: How did war, boom and depression change what Americans expected from their government and their nation's role in the world?

title: Twentieth-Century Crises

chapters.title: The Great War
chapters.bigQuestion: Why did the United States join a war across the ocean, and how did that war change life at home?

story.title: Old Tactics Meet New Weapons
story.kicker: In 1914, soldiers marched off expecting a short war. They found a long line of ditches instead.
paragraphs: In August 1914, crowds in Paris, Berlin and London cheered as soldiers marched off to war. Many young men believed the fighting would be over in a few months. Their generals planned the war the old way. Soldiers would charge forward in great waves. Horse soldiers would ride through the gaps. Brave men would win quick victories.

That is not what happened. The armies had new weapons that changed everything. A single machine gun could fire hundreds of bullets a minute. Big guns called artillery could fire shells for miles. When soldiers charged across open ground, most never got close to the enemy. Within months, both sides stopped running and started digging.

By the end of 1914, two lines of trenches stretched across Belgium and France, from the North Sea to the border of Switzerland. This was called the Western Front. The trenches were deep ditches, lined with sandbags and wooden boards. Soldiers ate, slept and stood guard in them. Rain turned the bottoms to mud. Rats and lice were everywhere. Between the two lines lay a strip of torn-up land called no man's land.

Generals kept trying to break through. They ordered huge attacks, sometimes after days of shelling. Again and again, the attackers were cut down. In 1916, the Battle of the Somme lasted about five months. More than a million soldiers were killed or wounded. The front line moved only a few miles. Inventors raced to find an answer: poison gas, tanks, airplanes. Each new weapon made the war deadlier, but none ended it quickly.

Some moments showed that the soldiers were still human beings. On Christmas 1914, in a few places along the line, British and German soldiers climbed out of their trenches. They shook hands, traded small gifts and sang songs. The next day, the war went on. It would last almost four more years, and in 1917 it would pull in the United States.
story.think: Why do you think generals kept using old tactics even after new weapons made them so deadly?

lessons.title: Four Roots of War
lessons.mainIdea: Militarism, alliances, imperialism and nationalism turned Europe into a place where one spark could start a huge war.
reading: By 1914, the great powers of Europe did not trust one another. Four forces built up tension over many years. Historians often remember them as four roots of the war. Each one alone might not have caused a world war. Together, they made one far more likely.

The first was *militarism*, the belief that a nation needs a large, strong military. Germany and Britain raced to build the biggest navy. Countries drew up detailed plans for war and kept millions of soldiers ready. The second was *alliances*. Nations made deals to defend each other. France, Russia and Britain lined up on one side. Germany and Austria-Hungary lined up on the other.

The third root was *imperialism*, when a strong nation takes control of other lands. European countries competed for colonies in Africa and Asia. Each new colony caused jealousy and quarrels. The fourth root was *nationalism*, a strong pride in one's own nation. Pride made leaders unwilling to back down. It also made some groups, like Serbs living inside Austria-Hungary, want their own country.

Together, these forces made Europe like a room full of gunpowder. Alliances meant that a fight between two countries could quickly pull in many more. Only a spark was needed. In the summer of 1914, that spark came in a city in southeastern Europe.

words.d: the belief that a nation should build a strong military and be ready to use it
an agreement between nations to help and defend each other
when a powerful nation takes control of other lands and peoples
strong pride in and loyalty to one's own nation or people

look.title: A Chain of Promises
look.text: Imagine five classmates. Two have promised to back each other up in any argument. The other three have made the same promise. One day, one student bumps another in the hall. Before long, all five are in the argument, even though most of them saw nothing.
look.prompt: How is this like the alliances in Europe in 1914? What might have stopped the argument from spreading?

check.q: What is militarism?
choices: The belief that a nation should build a strong military
A deal between two countries to trade goods
Strong pride in one's own nation
check.why: Militarism means building up a big military and being ready to use it.

check.q: Why did alliances make a small conflict more dangerous?
choices: Alliances banned all armies in Europe
Nations had promised to defend each other, so more countries would join in
Alliances only covered trade, not war
check.why: Because of their promises, allies could be pulled into a war that began between two other countries.

check.q: Which example shows nationalism?
choices: France and Russia signing a defense deal
Serbs in Austria-Hungary wanting their own country
check.why: Nationalism is strong pride in one's own people, which made many Serbs want their own nation.

lessons.title: The Spark at Sarajevo
lessons.mainIdea: The killing of Austria-Hungary's Archduke Franz Ferdinand in 1914 set off a chain of war declarations across Europe.
reading: On June 28, 1914, Archduke Franz Ferdinand rode through the city of Sarajevo in an open car. He was next in line to rule Austria-Hungary. A young Serbian nationalist named Gavrilo Princip shot and killed the archduke and his wife, Sophie. Princip wanted lands with Serbian people to break free from Austria-Hungary.

Austria-Hungary blamed Serbia and declared war on it. Then the alliances took over. Russia, a friend of Serbia, got its army ready. Germany, Austria-Hungary's ally, declared war on Russia and then on France. When German troops marched through neutral Belgium to reach France, Britain declared war on Germany. All of this happened in about one week in early August.

Two sides formed. The *Allies* included France, Britain and Russia. Italy joined them in 1915. The *Central Powers* included Germany, Austria-Hungary, the Ottoman Empire and Bulgaria. Colonies around the world were pulled in too. People at the time called it the Great War. Later it became known as World War I.

words.d: in World War I, the side that included France, Britain, Russia and later Italy and the United States
in World War I, the side that included Germany, Austria-Hungary, the Ottoman Empire and Bulgaria
not taking either side in a war or argument

look.title: One Week in August
look.text: In late July 1914, most Europeans were planning summer vacations. By the second week of August, five great powers were at war. Leaders later said that once armies started moving, their plans made it very hard to stop.
look.prompt: Why can a detailed war plan make it harder for leaders to choose peace?

check.q: Who was killed in Sarajevo on June 28, 1914?
check.why: Franz Ferdinand, heir to the throne of Austria-Hungary, was shot by Gavrilo Princip.

check.q: Why did Britain declare war on Germany?
choices: German troops marched through neutral Belgium
Germany sank a British ship in Sarajevo
Germany refused to trade with the United States
check.why: Germany invaded neutral Belgium to reach France, and Britain went to war.

check.q: Which nations were Central Powers?
choices: Germany, Austria-Hungary, the Ottoman Empire and Bulgaria
check.why: The Central Powers were Germany, Austria-Hungary, the Ottoman Empire and Bulgaria.

lessons.title: A New Kind of War
lessons.mainIdea: Machine guns, artillery, poison gas and other new weapons led to trench warfare and terrible losses with little gain.
reading: On the Western Front, the war became a *stalemate*. That means neither side could win. Soldiers lived in *trenches* for months at a time. Attacks across no man's land usually failed, because defenders with machine guns could stop them.

Both sides tried new weapons to break the deadlock. In 1915, Germany used poison gas, and soon both sides did. Soldiers had to carry gas masks. Britain rolled out the first tanks in 1916. They were slow and often broke down, but they could crush barbed wire and cross trenches.

The war also moved into the sky and under the sea. At first, airplanes scouted enemy lines. Soon pilots fought each other in the air. At sea, German submarines, called U-boats, sank ships carrying supplies to Britain. Submarines would later help bring the United States into the war.

The cost was enormous. By the end, about 9 million soldiers had died, along with millions of civilians. A whole generation of young men in France, Britain and Germany was scarred. People asked how their leaders could let so many die for so little ground.

words.d: a situation where neither side can win or move forward
a long, deep ditch that protects soldiers from enemy fire
a German submarine; the name comes from the German word for undersea boat

look.title: Weapon and Answer
look.text: Each new weapon brought an answer. Gas brought gas masks. Tanks brought anti-tank guns. Airplanes brought anti-aircraft guns. Submarines brought ships sailing together in groups, guarded by warships.
look.prompt: Why do you think new weapons did not end the war quickly, even though each one was powerful?

check.q: What does stalemate mean?
choices: One side wins a quick victory
Two armies agree to stop fighting
Neither side can win or move forward
check.why: A stalemate is a deadlock where neither side can make progress.

check.q: Why did most attacks across no man's land fail?
choices: Soldiers were not allowed to leave the trenches
The land was covered by water all year
Defenders with machine guns could stop soldiers crossing open ground
check.why: Machine guns made it almost impossible to cross open ground under fire.

check.q: What were U-boats?
check.why: U-boats were German submarines that attacked ships at sea.

lessons.title: Neutral in Name
lessons.mainIdea: President Wilson wanted the United States to stay neutral, but trade, loans and old ties pulled Americans toward the Allies.
reading: When the war began, President Woodrow Wilson said the United States would stay *neutral*. Most Americans agreed. The war seemed far away. Many people did not want to send their sons to fight in Europe's quarrels.

Yet Americans had strong feelings. About one in three Americans had been born abroad or had a parent who was. Many German Americans and Irish Americans were against Britain. Many other Americans felt close to Britain and France through language, history and democracy.

Money mattered too. American farms and factories sold huge amounts of food, steel and weapons to the Allies. Banks loaned the Allies billions of dollars. Britain's navy blocked most trade with Germany, so the Central Powers got much less. Over time, America's business was tied to an Allied victory.

British *propaganda* also shaped opinion. Britain cut Germany's undersea telegraph cables, so most war news reached America through British sources. Stories of German cruelty in Belgium, some true and some exaggerated, turned many Americans against Germany.

words.d: not taking either side in a war or argument
information, often one-sided, spread to shape people's opinions
money lent that must be paid back

look.title: Wilson Asks for Neutrality
look.text: The United States must be neutral in fact as well as in name during these days that are to try men's souls. We must be impartial in thought as well as in action…
look.cite: President Woodrow Wilson, message to the Senate, August 19, 1914
look.prompt: Wilson asked Americans to be neutral even in their thoughts. Why would that be hard for many Americans?

check.q: What did President Wilson declare when the war began in 1914?
choices: The United States would join the Allies
The United States would stay neutral
The United States would join the Central Powers
The United States would stop all trade
check.why: Wilson announced that the United States would be neutral.

check.q: How did trade tie the United States to the Allies?
choices: Americans sold goods only to Germany
The United States refused to trade with anyone
Americans sold goods and loaned money mostly to the Allies
The Allies paid Americans not to trade
check.why: Because Britain blocked trade with Germany, most U.S. sales and loans went to the Allies.

check.q: Why did most war news in America come from British sources?
choices: American reporters were banned from Europe
Britain cut Germany's undersea telegraph cables
check.why: With Germany's cables cut, news traveled mainly through Britain.

lessons.title: Submarines and a Secret Telegram
lessons.mainIdea: German submarine attacks and the Zimmermann Telegram turned many Americans against Germany.
reading: Germany used U-boats to stop supplies from reaching Britain. On May 7, 1915, a U-boat sank the British passenger ship *Lusitania* off the coast of Ireland. Nearly 1,200 people died, including 128 Americans. Americans were furious. Germany said the ship carried weapons, which was partly true, but most of the dead were ordinary travelers.

Wilson protested strongly. For a while, Germany promised to stop sinking passenger and merchant ships without warning. Wilson won reelection in 1916. Many voters liked that he had kept the country out of war.

Then, in early 1917, Germany took a gamble. It announced *unrestricted submarine warfare*. U-boats would sink any ship near Britain, even American ships. German leaders hoped to starve Britain before America could make a difference.

At the same time, British spies decoded a secret message from Germany's foreign minister, Arthur Zimmermann. He asked Mexico to join Germany if the United States entered the war. In return, Mexico could win back land it had lost to the United States. The message was printed in American newspapers in March 1917. Anger swept the country.

words.d: a British passenger ship sunk by a German submarine in 1915
a policy of sinking any ship in a war zone without warning
a message sent quickly over wires as a code of signals

look.title: The Zimmermann Telegram
look.text: …we make Mexico a proposal of alliance on the following basis: make war together, make peace together, generous financial support and an understanding on our part that Mexico is to reconquer the lost territory in Texas, New Mexico, and Arizona.
look.cite: Arthur Zimmermann, German foreign minister, telegram to Mexico, January 1917 (English translation)
look.prompt: Why would this message make Americans in the Southwest especially angry?

check.q: What happened to the Lusitania in 1915?
choices: It was sunk by a German U-boat
It carried the first U.S. soldiers to France
It brought the Zimmermann Telegram to America
check.why: A German submarine sank the Lusitania, killing nearly 1,200 people, including 128 Americans.

check.q: What did the Zimmermann Telegram propose?
choices: That Britain and Germany make peace
That Mexico join Germany and win back lost land
That the United States buy Mexico
check.why: Germany offered to help Mexico regain Texas, New Mexico and Arizona if it joined the war.

check.q: Why did Germany choose unrestricted submarine warfare in 1917?
choices: It wanted to protect American ships
It had signed a peace treaty
It hoped to starve Britain before America could make a difference
Its submarines could no longer fire
check.why: German leaders gambled that they could defeat Britain quickly, even if America joined.

lessons.title: Safe for Democracy
lessons.mainIdea: In April 1917, Wilson asked Congress for war, saying the fight would help make the world safe for democracy.
reading: In March 1917, U-boats sank several American ships. The same month, a revolution in Russia removed the czar, its all-powerful ruler. Now all the major Allies had some kind of elected government. That made it easier for Wilson to call the war a fight for *democracy*.

On April 2, 1917, Wilson spoke to Congress. He asked lawmakers to declare war on Germany. He said America had no selfish goals. It wanted no land and no payment. It would fight for the rights of people everywhere.

On April 6, 1917, Congress voted for war. Most members agreed, but some voted no. Jeannette Rankin of Montana, the first woman elected to Congress, was one of them. She said she wanted to stand by her country but could not vote for war.

The United States had a small army. It would take many months to build a large one and ship it across the Atlantic. The Allies were exhausted. They needed American soldiers, food and money as fast as possible.

words.d: government in which the people rule, usually by voting for leaders
to officially announce that a nation is at war; in the U.S., Congress has this power
the title of the emperor of Russia before 1917

look.title: Wilson's War Message
look.text: The world must be made safe for democracy. Its peace must be planted upon the tested foundations of political liberty.
look.cite: President Woodrow Wilson, address to Congress, April 2, 1917
look.prompt: What reason for war does Wilson give here? Why might this reason appeal to Americans more than revenge?

check.q: When did Congress declare war on Germany?
check.why: Wilson asked for war on April 2, 1917, and Congress voted on April 6.

check.q: How did the Russian Revolution of March 1917 help Wilson's argument?
choices: It removed the czar, so the Allies looked more like democracies
It made Russia join the Central Powers
It ended the war in Europe
check.why: With the czar gone, Wilson could more easily describe the Allies as fighting for democracy.

check.q: Who was Jeannette Rankin?
choices: A nurse who served in France
The first woman in Congress, who voted against the war
The leader of the Allied armies
A German spy caught in Texas
check.why: Rankin, from Montana, was the first woman elected to Congress and voted no on war.

lessons.title: Raising an Army
lessons.mainIdea: Through a draft, the United States built an army of millions and sent about 2 million soldiers to France.
reading: To build an army fast, Congress passed the Selective Service Act in May 1917. This created a *draft*, a system that requires people to serve in the military. Millions of men signed up on registration day. Numbers were drawn to decide who would go.

The soldiers were called the American Expeditionary Force, or *AEF*. General John J. Pershing led them. People nicknamed American soldiers “doughboys.” Soldiers came from farms, cities and immigrant neighborhoods. Some did not yet speak English well.

The army was *segregated*, meaning Black and white soldiers served in separate units. More than 350,000 African Americans served. Many were given only labor jobs. But some Black units fought bravely. The 369th Infantry from New York, called the Harlem Hellfighters, fought alongside French troops. The 370th Infantry, first formed as the 8th Illinois National Guard, came from Chicago and had Black officers.

Native Americans served too, even though many were not yet U.S. citizens. Women served as nurses and as telephone operators in France. Their service helped change ideas about who belonged in the nation.

words.d: a system that requires people to serve in the military
the American Expeditionary Force, the U.S. Army sent to Europe in World War I
separated by race, by law or by custom

look.title: Building an Army, 1917–1918
rows: Men who registered for the draft
look.cite: U.S. Selective Service and War Department records, rounded
look.prompt: About what fraction of the men who registered were actually drafted? What does that tell you?

check.q: What did the Selective Service Act of 1917 create?
choices: A draft to build the army
check.why: The act created a draft that required men to register for military service.

check.q: Who led the American Expeditionary Force?
check.why: General John J. Pershing commanded the AEF in France.

check.q: What was special about Chicago's 370th Infantry?
choices: It was a Black unit that had Black officers
It was the first tank unit
It was made up of women
check.why: The 370th, formed from the 8th Illinois National Guard, was an African American unit led by Black officers.

lessons.title: Over There
lessons.mainIdea: Fresh American troops helped the Allies stop Germany's last big attack and push forward until the armistice of November 11, 1918.
reading: American troops arrived in large numbers in 1918, just in time. Russia had left the war after a second revolution. That let Germany move soldiers to the Western Front. In spring 1918, Germany launched huge attacks and pushed toward Paris.

American soldiers and Marines helped stop the Germans at Château-Thierry and Belleau Wood in June 1918. Then the Allies struck back. In the fall, more than a million Americans fought in the Meuse-Argonne Offensive in France. It was the largest battle in American history up to that time.

Germany was running out of soldiers, food and hope. Its people were hungry and angry. On November 11, 1918, at 11 a.m., an *armistice* took effect. That is an agreement to stop fighting. Church bells rang across Europe and America.

About 116,000 Americans died in the war. More than half died from disease, not battle. Their sacrifice was smaller than that of France or Britain, but the fresh American troops had tipped the balance.

words.d: an agreement to stop fighting
a large planned attack by an army

look.title: Why Timing Mattered
look.text: By 1918, French and British armies had been fighting for almost four years. Germany had just freed up many soldiers after Russia left the war. Then hundreds of thousands of fresh, well-fed American soldiers began arriving every month.
look.prompt: How might the arrival of fresh troops change the feelings of both the Allies and the Germans?

check.q: What is an armistice?
choices: A tax to pay for war
check.why: An armistice is an agreement to stop fighting; World War I's took effect on November 11, 1918.

check.q: Why could Germany send more soldiers to the Western Front in 1918?
check.why: After Russia left the war, Germany moved troops from the east to the west.

check.q: What killed more than half of the Americans who died in World War I?
check.why: More than half of the roughly 116,000 American deaths came from disease, especially influenza.

sections.title: The Home Front and the Peace

lessons.title: Selling the War
lessons.mainIdea: The government raised money, shaped opinion and limited free speech to win support for the war.
reading: War is expensive. The government sold *Liberty Bonds*, loans from ordinary people that would be paid back with interest. Movie stars held rallies. Children bought savings stamps. The government also raised taxes on high incomes.

To win hearts, Wilson created the Committee on Public Information, led by George Creel. It made posters, films and pamphlets. Thousands of volunteer speakers gave short talks in movie theaters. Some of this *propaganda* also spread fear and hatred of Germans.

German Americans faced suspicion and cruelty. Some schools stopped teaching German. Sauerkraut was renamed “liberty cabbage.” In Collinsville, Illinois, in 1918, a mob killed a German-born man named Robert Prager, who was falsely accused of disloyalty.

Congress passed the Espionage Act in 1917 and the Sedition Act in 1918. These laws made it a crime to interfere with the draft or, later, to criticize the government or the war in harsh ways. Labor leader Eugene V. Debs was sent to prison for a speech against the war. In 1920 he ran for president from his prison cell and won nearly a million votes.

words.d: loans that Americans made to the government to pay for World War I
information, often one-sided, spread to shape people's opinions
speech or action that urges people to rebel against the government

look.title: The Supreme Court on Free Speech in Wartime
look.text: The most stringent protection of free speech would not protect a man in falsely shouting fire in a theatre and causing a panic.
look.cite: Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr., Schenck v. United States, 1919
look.prompt: Holmes says free speech has limits. Where do you think the line should be during a war?

check.q: What were Liberty Bonds?
choices: Loans from Americans to the government to pay for the war
Posters that urged men to enlist
check.why: Liberty Bonds let ordinary people lend money to the government for the war.

check.q: What did the Espionage and Sedition Acts do?
choices: Made it a crime to interfere with the draft or harshly criticize the war
Allowed soldiers to vote by mail
check.why: These laws limited speech and actions seen as hurting the war effort.

check.q: Why was Eugene V. Debs sent to prison?
choices: He refused to buy Liberty Bonds
He gave a speech against the war
check.why: Debs was convicted under the wartime laws for a speech opposing the war.

lessons.title: New Jobs, New Journeys
lessons.mainIdea: The war opened factory jobs to women and to African Americans, starting the Great Migration from the South to Northern cities like Chicago.
reading: With millions of men in uniform and immigration from Europe cut off, factories needed workers. Women took jobs in factories, offices and railroads. Many had never been paid for work outside the home before. Their war work helped win support for the *19th Amendment*, which gave women the right to vote in 1920.

African Americans in the South faced Jim Crow laws, low pay and violence. Now Northern factories were hiring. Hundreds of thousands of Black Southerners moved north. This movement became known as the *Great Migration*. It continued for decades.

Chicago was a top destination. The Chicago Defender, a Black newspaper, urged Southerners to come north. Pullman porters on the trains carried copies south. The Illinois Central Railroad ran straight from Mississippi and Louisiana to Chicago. New arrivals found work in the stockyards, steel mills and rail yards.

The North was not free of prejudice. Black families faced unfair housing rules and hostility. In July 1919, a Black teenager named Eugene Williams drowned after being attacked at a Chicago beach. Days of rioting followed, and 38 people died. The violence showed how deep the racial divide ran.

words.d: the movement of millions of African Americans from the South to cities in the North and West, beginning around 1916
the 1920 change to the Constitution that gave women the right to vote

look.title: African Americans Living in Chicago
look.cite: U.S. Census Bureau, rounded
look.prompt: Between which two census years did Chicago's Black population grow the most? What events help explain it?

check.q: What was the Great Migration?
choices: The trip of U.S. soldiers to France
The move of farmers to the Great Plains
The movement of African Americans from the South to Northern and Western cities
check.why: Beginning around 1916, millions of Black Southerners moved north and west for jobs and freedom.

check.q: How did the Chicago Defender help the Great Migration?
choices: It urged Black Southerners to move north
It built factories in the South
check.why: The Black-owned newspaper encouraged Southerners to come to Chicago for work and a better life.

check.q: Why did Northern factories need new workers during the war?
choices: Men went to war and immigration from Europe was cut off
Farm jobs paid more than factory jobs
check.why: With men in the army and few immigrants arriving, factories hired women and Black workers.

lessons.title: The Deadly Flu of 1918
lessons.mainIdea: A worldwide flu pandemic in 1918 and 1919 killed far more Americans than the war did.
reading: In 1918, a new kind of *influenza*, or flu, spread around the world. It moved fast in crowded army camps and on troop ships. Soldiers carried it from place to place. Unlike most flus, it was especially deadly for healthy young adults.

A *pandemic* is a disease that spreads across many countries. The 1918 flu reached almost every part of the world. It killed at least 50 million people worldwide. In the United States, about 675,000 people died.

Cities tried to slow it down. Many closed schools, theaters and churches. People were told to wear masks and avoid crowds. Nurses and doctors worked until they dropped. There were no vaccines or medicines that could cure it.
Because of the war, many governments kept news of the flu quiet at first. They did not want to hurt morale. Scientists today still study the 1918 pandemic to prepare for new diseases.

words.d: a disease caused by a virus that spreads easily, often called the flu
an outbreak of disease that spreads across many countries or the whole world
the level of hope and confidence in a group of people

look.title: American Deaths: War and Flu
rows: U.S. soldiers killed in battle, WWI
look.cite: U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs and Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, rounded
look.prompt: About how many times more Americans died from the flu than in the war?

check.q: What is a pandemic?
choices: A disease outbreak that spreads across many countries
check.why: A pandemic is a disease that spreads across many countries or the world.

check.q: About how many Americans died in the flu pandemic?
check.why: About 675,000 Americans died; about 50 million or more died worldwide.

check.q: Why did the flu spread so quickly in 1918?
choices: Crowded army camps and troop ships helped it move
It was spread only by animals
check.why: War brought people together in crowded camps and ships, which helped the virus spread.

lessons.title: Winning the War, Losing the Peace
lessons.mainIdea: Wilson hoped for a fair peace and a League of Nations, but the Treaty of Versailles punished Germany and the U.S. Senate rejected the League.
reading: In January 1918, Wilson listed his goals for peace, called the Fourteen Points. He wanted open agreements, free trade, fewer weapons and the right of peoples to choose their own governments. His last point called for a *League of Nations*, a group where countries could settle disputes without war.

In 1919, leaders met near Paris. Britain and France wanted Germany to pay. The *Treaty of Versailles*, signed on June 28, 1919, forced Germany to accept blame for the war. It had to pay huge sums called *reparations*, give up land and shrink its army. New nations such as Poland and Czechoslovakia appeared on the map. The treaty did create the League of Nations.

Back home, the Senate had to approve the treaty. Senator Henry Cabot Lodge and others worried the League could drag America into future wars without a vote of Congress. Wilson refused to compromise. He toured the country to win support, but he suffered a stroke in 1919.

The Senate never approved the treaty. The United States never joined the League. Many Germans felt the treaty was unfair and humiliating. That anger would help bring about an even bigger war twenty years later.

words.d: a world organization formed after World War I to help keep peace
the 1919 peace treaty that ended World War I with Germany
payments a defeated nation must make for war damage

look.text: A general association of nations must be formed under specific covenants for the purpose of affording mutual guarantees of political independence and territorial integrity to great and small states alike.
look.cite: President Woodrow Wilson, Fourteen Points address to Congress, January 8, 1918
look.prompt: In your own words, what would this association of nations promise its members? Why did some senators worry about that promise?

check.q: What did Wilson's Fourteen Points call for in the last point?
check.why: The fourteenth point called for an association of nations, which became the League of Nations.

check.q: How did the Treaty of Versailles treat Germany?
choices: It let Germany keep all its land and army
It made Germany a member of the Allies
It blamed Germany and made it pay reparations and give up land
check.why: The treaty forced Germany to accept blame, pay reparations, lose land and shrink its army.

check.q: Why did many senators oppose joining the League of Nations?
choices: They wanted Germany to lead it
They thought it was too weak to matter
They wanted to rejoin the war
They feared it could pull the U.S. into wars without Congress's vote
check.why: Critics like Henry Cabot Lodge worried League promises could commit America to future wars.

choices: The killing of Archduke Franz Ferdinand
review.why: The assassination in Sarajevo in June 1914 set off the chain of war declarations.

review.q: Why did the war on the Western Front become a stalemate?
choices: Machine guns and trenches made attacks fail

review.why: Defenders in trenches with machine guns could stop almost any attack across open ground.

choices: The Treaty of Versailles and the flu

choices: To make the world safe for democracy
review.why: Wilson said America sought no land or payment and would fight so the world would be safe for democracy.

review.q: How did the government limit speech during the war?
choices: It passed the Espionage and Sedition Acts
It ended the right to vote

review.why: An armistice, or agreement to stop fighting, took effect that day; the treaty came later.

choices: Every state voted to approve it
The Senate refused to approve it
review.why: The Senate never ratified the treaty, and the United States never joined the League of Nations.

chapters.title: The Roaring Twenties
chapters.bigQuestion: Were the 1920s a time of new freedom and fun, a time of fear and division, or both at once?

story.title: A Trumpet on the South Side
story.kicker: In 1922, a young horn player from New Orleans stepped off a train in Chicago and helped change American music.
paragraphs: In the summer of 1922, a 21-year-old musician named Louis Armstrong rode a train north from New Orleans to Chicago. He carried his horn and a telegram. It came from his hero, Joe “King” Oliver, a famous bandleader. Oliver wanted Armstrong to join his Creole Jazz Band. Armstrong had grown up poor in New Orleans, and he had never lived anywhere else.

The Chicago he found was booming. Hundreds of thousands of African Americans had come north in the Great Migration. Many settled on the city's South Side, in a neighborhood that later became known as Bronzeville. It had Black-owned stores, churches, banks, theaters and the Chicago Defender newspaper. Newcomers from Mississippi, Louisiana and Alabama brought their food, their faith and their music with them.

That music was jazz. It grew out of the blues, ragtime, church songs and brass bands of the South. Its players often made up melodies on the spot. This is called improvising. At the Lincoln Gardens dance hall, Oliver and Armstrong played two horns together so tightly that listeners were amazed. Young white musicians came to listen and learn. Dancers packed the floor late into the night.

In 1923, Oliver's band made records, among the first ever made by a Black jazz band. Then, from 1925 to 1928, Armstrong recorded in Chicago with his own groups, the Hot Five and Hot Seven. His bold solos and warm, rough singing voice changed how people played and sang. Records and radio carried jazz into homes across the country. People began calling the whole decade the Jazz Age.

Life on the South Side was not easy. Unfair housing rules kept most Black families from moving to other neighborhoods, so homes were crowded and rents were high. Still, the South Side was a place of pride and creativity. From its clubs, a new American sound spread around the world.
story.think: Why do you think music that began in the South became a national sensation after it moved north to cities like Chicago?

lessons.title: A Return to Normal
lessons.mainIdea: Tired of war and reform, voters chose Republican presidents who promised calm, low taxes and help for business.
reading: By 1920, many Americans were worn out. They had lived through a world war, a deadly flu and bitter strikes. Warren G. Harding, a Republican senator from Ohio, promised a return to “normalcy.” He won the 1920 election easily.

Harding picked some honest, skilled advisers. But he also gave jobs to friends who used their power to get rich. In the worst *scandal*, called Teapot Dome, Interior Secretary Albert Fall took bribes. In return, he let private companies drill on government oil land. Fall became the first cabinet member sent to prison. Harding died in 1923 before most of the scandal came out.

Vice President Calvin Coolidge became president. People called him “Silent Cal” because he spoke so little. Coolidge believed government should stay small and let business grow. Taxes were cut, especially for the wealthy. Coolidge won the 1924 election. In 1928, voters chose another Republican, Herbert Hoover, for president.

Supporters said these policies brought jobs and prosperity. Critics said they helped the rich far more than farmers and workers. Both views would matter when the good times ended. People still argue about how much these choices helped cause the troubles of the 1930s.

words.d: Harding's word for a calm, ordinary time without war or big changes
an action or event that is wrong or dishonest and causes public anger
a time of economic success, with good jobs and rising wealth

look.title: Harding's Promise
look.text: America's present need is not heroics, but healing; not nostrums, but normalcy; not revolution, but restoration; not agitation, but adjustment…
look.cite: Warren G. Harding, speech in Boston, May 14, 1920
look.prompt: A nostrum is a quick-fix cure. Why would this message appeal to voters in 1920?

check.q: What did Warren G. Harding promise voters in 1920?
choices: Joining the League of Nations right away
check.why: Harding promised a calm return to normal life after the war.

check.q: What was the Teapot Dome scandal?
choices: A strike by tea workers in Boston
An official took bribes to let companies drill on government oil land
A fight over a new tax on tea
check.why: Albert Fall took bribes in exchange for leases on government oil reserves.

check.q: What did Calvin Coolidge believe about government?
choices: It should run all the factories
It should raise taxes on everyone
It should stay small and let business grow
check.why: Coolidge favored small government, low taxes and support for business.

lessons.title: The Red Scare
lessons.mainIdea: After the Russian Revolution, fear of communism led to raids, arrests and deportations that ignored many people's rights.
reading: In 1917, *communists* took power in Russia. Communists wanted workers to overthrow owners and have the government control property. They said their revolution would spread. Many Americans feared it might spread to the United States.

In 1919, more than 4 million American workers went on strike for better pay. Police officers in Boston even walked off the job. That year, bombs were mailed to government leaders. One exploded at the home of Attorney General A. Mitchell Palmer. Fear of radicals, people who want extreme change, grew into a *Red Scare*. Red was the color of communism.

In late 1919 and early 1920, Palmer's agents raided offices and homes in many cities. Thousands were arrested, often without proof of any crime. Many were immigrants. Hundreds were deported, or sent out of the country. Critics said the raids trampled on free speech and fair trials.

In 1920, two Italian immigrants, Nicola Sacco and Bartolomeo Vanzetti, were arrested for a robbery and murder. They were anarchists, people who oppose all government. They were convicted and executed in 1927. Many people then and since have doubted they received a fair trial.

words.d: a person who believes the government should own property and businesses for all the people
a period of intense fear of communists and radicals in the United States
to force a person who is not a citizen to leave the country

look.title: Fear and Fairness
look.text: Imagine that someone in your town set off a bomb. The police respond by arresting hundreds of people from one immigrant group. Most have done nothing wrong, but they share some political ideas with the bomber.
look.prompt: How can a nation protect itself from real dangers without punishing innocent people?

check.q: What caused the Red Scare?
choices: Fear that a communist revolution would spread to America
check.why: After communists took power in Russia, strikes and bombings made many Americans fear revolution.

check.q: What were the Palmer Raids?
choices: Government raids that arrested thousands of suspected radicals
check.why: Attorney General Palmer's agents arrested thousands, often without evidence.

check.q: Why did many people question the Sacco and Vanzetti case?
choices: They doubted the two men got a fair trial
The trial happened in secret in Russia
check.why: Many believed prejudice against immigrants and radicals shaped the trial.

lessons.title: Closing the Door
lessons.mainIdea: New laws in the 1920s set quotas that sharply limited immigration, especially from southern and eastern Europe and Asia.
reading: Before the war, about a million immigrants a year came to the United States. Many came from Italy, Poland, Russia and Greece. Some Americans feared these newcomers. They said immigrants took jobs or brought dangerous ideas. Prejudice against Catholics and Jews was also strong.

Congress acted. A 1921 law created *quotas*, or limits, on how many people could come from each country. The Immigration Act of 1924 made the limits much tighter. Each nation's quota was based on how many people from that country lived in the U.S. in 1890. That was before most southern and eastern Europeans had arrived, so their quotas were tiny.

The 1924 law also blocked almost all immigration from Asia. Japan was deeply offended, because it saw the law as an insult to its people. Chinese immigrants had already been shut out since the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882.

The quotas did not apply to countries in the Americas. Many Mexican workers came north to work on farms and railroads. In 1924, Congress also created the U.S. Border Patrol. The quota system stayed in place until 1965.

words.d: a fixed limit on the number of people or things allowed
an unfair opinion about a group of people, formed without knowing them
a person who moves to a new country to live there

look.title: How the 1924 Quotas Worked
look.text: Each country's yearly quota will be 2 percent of the number of people born in that country who were living in the United States in 1890.
look.cite: Immigration Act of 1924 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Why did choosing the year 1890, instead of a later year, give Italy and Poland small quotas?

check.q: What is a quota?
choices: A fixed limit on a number
check.why: An immigration quota limited how many people could come from each country.

check.q: Why did the 1924 law use the 1890 census?
choices: Few southern and eastern Europeans lived in the U.S. then, so their quotas would be small
It was the most recent census
It was the year the Constitution was written
check.why: Using an earlier census kept the numbers from Italy, Poland and similar countries low.

check.q: Which group was NOT limited by the 1924 quotas?
choices: People from countries in the Americas, like Mexico
check.why: The quotas did not cover the Western Hemisphere, so Mexican immigration continued.

lessons.title: The Klan Returns
lessons.mainIdea: A new Ku Klux Klan grew to millions of members in the 1920s, spreading hate against Black Americans, Catholics, Jews and immigrants.
reading: The first Ku Klux Klan had used terror against Black Southerners during Reconstruction. In 1915, a new Klan was started in Georgia. In the 1920s it grew fast. At its peak, it had millions of members, in the North and West as well as the South.

The new Klan attacked anyone it saw as not truly “American.” It targeted African Americans, Catholics, Jews and immigrants. Members wore white robes and hoods and burned crosses to frighten people. Some Klan members used violence. The Klan also used politics. In Indiana and other states, it helped elect governors, mayors and lawmakers.

Many Americans spoke out against the Klan. Black newspapers, Catholic and Jewish groups, and immigrant communities pushed back. In 1925, a top Klan leader in Indiana was convicted of murder. People saw that the group claiming to protect morals was led by criminals.

After that, the Klan shrank quickly. The Klan never fully disappeared, but it lost most of its power. Its rise showed how much fear and *bigotry* existed in the 1920s, even in a time known for fun and new freedoms.

words.d: hatred of or strong unfairness toward people because of their race, religion or background
to frighten someone to force them to do or not do something

look.title: Why Hate Groups Grow
look.text: In the 1920s, America was changing fast. Cities were growing. Immigrants and Black migrants were moving in. Young people were acting in new ways. Some people felt their way of life was slipping away. The Klan told them that outsiders were to blame.
look.prompt: Why can blaming a group of people seem appealing during times of change? How can communities resist it?

check.q: Which groups did the Klan of the 1920s target?
choices: African Americans, Catholics, Jews and immigrants
check.why: The 1920s Klan spread hate against Black Americans, Catholics, Jews and immigrants.

check.q: How was the 1920s Klan different from the first Klan?
choices: It was strong in the North and West too, and active in politics
check.why: The new Klan spread nationwide and helped elect officials in states like Indiana.

check.q: What helped cause the Klan to shrink after 1925?
choices: A top leader was convicted of murder
Congress made it the official police
It merged with a labor union
check.why: The Indiana leader's murder conviction exposed the Klan's crimes and hypocrisy.

lessons.title: Prohibition
lessons.mainIdea: The 18th Amendment banned alcohol, but many people broke the law, and illegal liquor helped gangsters grow rich and powerful.
reading: For many years, the temperance movement had worked to limit alcohol. Temperance means drinking little or no alcohol. Supporters said drinking hurt families, health and work. Frances Willard of Evanston, Illinois, led the Woman's Christian Temperance Union and made it a national force.

In 1919, the states ratified the 18th Amendment. Starting in January 1920, making, selling or shipping alcoholic drinks was illegal. This era was called *Prohibition*. Drinking went down at first, especially in rural areas.

But millions of people ignored the law. They went to hidden bars called *speakeasies*. *Bootleggers* smuggled liquor from Canada and the Caribbean or made it in secret. Gangs fought over the profits. In Chicago, Al Capone ran a huge illegal liquor business and was linked to many killings. He was finally sent to prison in 1931, for not paying taxes.

Many Americans decided Prohibition caused more harm than good. It made criminals rich and taught people to ignore the law. In 1933, the 21st Amendment repealed, or canceled, the 18th Amendment. It is the only amendment ever repealed.

words.d: the period from 1920 to 1933 when making and selling alcohol was illegal in the U.S.
a hidden bar that sold alcohol illegally during Prohibition
a person who made, carried or sold alcohol illegally
to cancel a law

look.title: The 18th Amendment
look.text: …the manufacture, sale, or transportation of intoxicating liquors within, the importation thereof into, or the exportation thereof from the United States … for beverage purposes is hereby prohibited.
look.cite: U.S. Constitution, 18th Amendment, Section 1, ratified 1919
look.prompt: Notice that the amendment bans making and selling alcohol, but not drinking it. Why might that matter?

check.q: What did the 18th Amendment do?
choices: Gave women the right to vote
Banned making, selling and shipping alcoholic drinks
check.why: The 18th Amendment began Prohibition in 1920.

check.q: How did Prohibition help gangsters like Al Capone?
choices: It made them leave the country
Illegal liquor sales made them rich and powerful
check.why: Because alcohol was illegal but still wanted, gangs made huge profits selling it.

check.q: How did Prohibition end?
choices: The Supreme Court banned it in 1920
check.why: The 21st Amendment canceled the 18th, the only amendment ever repealed.

lessons.title: Science and Faith on Trial
lessons.mainIdea: The 1925 Scopes trial over teaching evolution showed a sharp divide between traditional religious values and modern ideas.
reading: In 1925, Tennessee passed a law called the Butler Act. It banned public school teachers from teaching that humans developed from earlier forms of life. This idea is part of the scientific theory of *evolution*.

A civil liberties group offered to defend any teacher who would test the law in court. John Scopes, a young science teacher in Dayton, Tennessee, agreed. He was charged with breaking the law. The trial in July 1925 became a national event. A Chicago radio station, WGN, broadcast it live.

Two famous men faced off. William Jennings Bryan, a three-time presidential candidate and a devout Christian, helped the prosecution. Clarence Darrow, a well-known Chicago lawyer, defended Scopes. In one famous moment, Darrow questioned Bryan himself about the Bible.

Scopes was found guilty and fined $100. A higher court later threw out the fine on a technical point. People saw the trial differently. Some felt it defended faith and the right of communities to decide what schools teach. Others felt it defended science and a teacher's freedom. The debate over *values* in schools continues today.

words.d: the scientific theory that living things change over long periods of time
the beliefs a person or group holds about what is right and important

look.title: Tennessee's Butler Act
look.text: …it shall be unlawful for any teacher … to teach any theory that denies the story of the Divine Creation of man as taught in the Bible, and to teach instead that man has descended from a lower order of animals.
look.cite: Tennessee Butler Act, 1925
look.prompt: Who should decide what is taught in public schools: parents, voters, lawmakers, scientists or teachers? Explain.

check.q: What was John Scopes charged with?
choices: Teaching evolution in a public school
check.why: Scopes was charged with breaking Tennessee's ban on teaching human evolution.

check.q: Who defended Scopes in court?
check.why: Chicago lawyer Clarence Darrow led the defense; Bryan helped the prosecution.

check.q: What larger conflict did the Scopes trial reveal?
choices: A fight between Britain and Germany
A divide between traditional religious values and modern ideas
A strike by teachers for higher pay
check.why: The trial showed deep disagreement over faith, science and who controls schools.

lessons.title: Cars and Credit
lessons.mainIdea: Mass-produced cars and buying on credit changed how Americans lived, worked and spent money.
reading: In 1908, Henry Ford began selling the Model T. It was simple, tough and cheaper than most cars. In 1913, Ford's factory started using a moving *assembly line*. Workers stayed in one place while the car moved past them. Each worker did one small task. Building a car's frame and engine went from more than 12 hours to about an hour and a half.

Faster building meant lower prices. The Model T cost $850 in 1908. By the mid-1920s, it cost less than $300. In 1914, Ford also began paying many workers $5 a day, about double the usual pay. Now factory workers could afford the cars they built. Making huge numbers of goods this way is called *mass production*.
Cars changed the country. Towns paved roads and built gas stations. Families could live farther from work, and suburbs grew. Rural families could drive to town. Teenagers could go out on their own.

Americans also bought radios, washing machines and vacuum cleaners. Many paid on *credit*, using installment plans: a small payment now and more each month. Advertising urged people to buy now and pay later. This helped the economy grow, but it also left many families in debt.

words.d: a way of making goods in which the product moves past workers who each do one task
making large numbers of the same product quickly and cheaply
an arrangement to buy something now and pay for it later, usually with extra charges

look.title: Passenger Cars Registered in the U.S.
look.cite: U.S. Federal Highway Administration, rounded
look.prompt: About how many times more cars were there in 1929 than in 1920? What changes would so many cars bring?

check.q: How did the assembly line change car making?
choices: It meant each worker built a whole car
It stopped cars from being sold
It made cars much faster and cheaper to build
check.why: Moving the car past workers who each did one task cut building time and lowered prices.

check.q: What does buying on credit mean?
choices: Buying now and paying later in small payments
Getting items for free from the government
check.why: Installment credit let people take goods home and pay over time.

check.q: What was one effect of cars on American life?
choices: Suburbs grew because people could live farther from work
check.why: Cars let families live farther from jobs, helping suburbs grow.

lessons.title: Radio, Movies and Heroes
lessons.mainIdea: Radio, movies and sports created a shared national culture and made celebrities out of athletes and pilots.
reading: In 1920, station KDKA in Pittsburgh broadcast the results of the presidential election. It was one of the first commercial radio stations. Within ten years, millions of homes had a radio. Families gathered to hear news, music, comedy shows and ball games. For the first time, people across the country heard the same thing at the same moment.

Movies were even more popular. Millions of people went to the movies every week. Charlie Chaplin made audiences laugh in silent films. In 1927, The Jazz Singer became the first feature-length movie with spoken dialogue. Soon silent films were gone.

Americans loved sports heroes. Babe Ruth hit 60 home runs in 1927. Red Grange, the “Galloping Ghost” from Wheaton, Illinois, starred at the University of Illinois and then for the Chicago Bears. Such stars became *celebrities*, famous people followed by fans.

Pilots were heroes too. In May 1927, Charles Lindbergh flew alone, without stopping, from New York to Paris. Bessie Coleman, who lived in Chicago, became the first African American woman to earn a pilot's license, in 1921. She had to go to France to learn, because American flight schools would not accept her.

words.d: to send out programs by radio or television to a large audience
a famous person followed by many fans
entertainment and ideas shared by huge numbers of people at the same time

look.title: A Shared Culture
look.text: Before radio, a farm family in Iowa and a factory family in Chicago might never hear the same song or news story at the same time. By the late 1920s, both could sit by their radios and hear the same ball game, the same comedy show and the same advertisements.
look.prompt: How might hearing the same shows and ads change the way Americans thought, talked and shopped?

check.q: What made The Jazz Singer important?
choices: It was the first radio broadcast
It was the first color television show
It was the first feature-length movie with spoken dialogue
check.why: The Jazz Singer in 1927 brought talking pictures to feature films.

check.q: What did Charles Lindbergh do in 1927?
choices: Flew alone nonstop from New York to Paris
check.why: Lindbergh's solo nonstop flight across the Atlantic made him a hero.

check.q: Why did Bessie Coleman go to France to learn to fly?
choices: American flight schools would not accept her
France paid her to move there
She was in the army in France
check.why: Because of discrimination against her as a Black woman, she trained in France.

lessons.title: Flappers and New Freedoms
lessons.mainIdea: Young women in the 1920s gained the vote and new freedoms, though most women's lives changed more slowly than the flapper image suggests.
reading: In 1920, the 19th Amendment gave women the right to vote. Many women hoped this would lead to other changes. Some ran for office. A few were elected to state legislatures and to Congress.

Some young women, called *flappers*, broke old rules. They cut their hair short in a style called a bob and wore shorter skirts. They danced the Charleston, drove cars and went out without a chaperone, an older person who watched over them. Older Americans were often shocked.

More women worked outside the home, especially as typists, clerks, telephone operators, nurses and teachers. Most jobs still paid women less than men. Many women, especially Black and immigrant women, worked hard jobs as cooks, maids and factory hands, as they had before.

Most women were not flappers. Most married women still spent their days caring for homes and children. But new appliances made some chores easier. The image of the free, modern woman changed what many girls dreamed they could do.

words.d: a young woman of the 1920s who broke old rules about dress and behavior
an older person who goes along to watch over young people

look.title: Image and Reality
look.text: Magazines and movies of the 1920s were filled with flappers. A farm woman in rural Illinois, though, might still haul water, cook for a large family and have no electricity in her home.
look.prompt: Why do you think the flapper became the famous image of the 1920s, even though most women did not live that way?

check.q: Who were flappers?
choices: Pilots who flew across the ocean
Young women who broke old rules about dress and behavior
check.why: Flappers wore short hair and skirts and claimed new social freedoms.

check.q: What did the 19th Amendment do?
choices: Gave women the right to vote
check.why: Ratified in 1920, the 19th Amendment gave women the vote.

check.q: Which statement about women in the 1920s is most accurate?
choices: Women were banned from all jobs
Some gained new freedoms, but most women's lives changed slowly
check.why: The flapper was a famous image, but most women still lived traditional lives.

lessons.title: Chicago's Black Metropolis
lessons.mainIdea: The Great Migration built a thriving Black community on Chicago's South Side, full of businesses, music and political power.
reading: The Great Migration kept going through the 1920s. Black Southerners came north to escape Jim Crow laws and find better jobs. Chicago's Black population more than doubled during the decade.

On the South Side, newcomers built what some called a Black *metropolis*, a city within a city. There were Black-owned banks, insurance companies, newspapers, stores and churches. Ida B. Wells, the famous journalist and civil rights leader, lived there and kept working for justice.

The South Side was also a center of jazz and blues. Musicians like Louis Armstrong and King Oliver played in its clubs. Records made in Chicago spread the music across the nation. Blues singers, church choirs and dance bands made the South Side one of the most exciting places in America.

Black Chicagoans gained political power too. In 1928, voters on the South Side elected Oscar De Priest to Congress. He was the first African American elected to Congress from a Northern state. But *discrimination* remained. Rules called restrictive covenants barred Black families from buying homes in many neighborhoods. That kept the South Side crowded.

words.d: a large, important city or city-like community
unfair treatment of people because of their race, religion or other group
a rule in a property deed that banned selling a home to certain groups

look.title: Opportunity and Limits
look.text: A family arrives in Chicago from Mississippi in 1925. The father finds a job in the stockyards that pays far more than farming did. The children go to school, and the family can vote. But when they try to rent a bigger apartment in another neighborhood, they are turned away.
look.prompt: In what ways was Chicago better than the South for this family? In what ways was it still unfair?

check.q: Who was Oscar De Priest?
choices: The first African American elected to Congress from a Northern state
check.why: South Side voters elected De Priest to Congress in 1928.

check.q: What were restrictive covenants?
choices: Rules that barred selling homes to certain groups
check.why: These property rules kept Black families out of many neighborhoods.

check.q: Why did Black Southerners keep moving to Chicago in the 1920s?
choices: Because the government forced them to
To escape Jim Crow laws and find better jobs
check.why: Jobs and more freedom drew migrants north, though they still faced discrimination.

lessons.title: The Harlem Renaissance
lessons.mainIdea: In the 1920s, Black writers, artists and musicians in Harlem created works that celebrated African American life and pride.
reading: Harlem is a neighborhood in New York City. By the 1920s, it had become one of the largest Black communities in the country. Writers, artists and musicians gathered there. Their burst of creative work is called the *Harlem Renaissance*. Renaissance means rebirth.

Langston Hughes was one of its brightest voices. He wrote poems in the rhythms of jazz and blues about the lives of ordinary Black people. Zora Neale Hurston, who grew up in an all-Black town in Florida, collected folk tales and wrote novels. Claude McKay and Countee Cullen wrote powerful poetry.

Music filled Harlem's clubs. Duke Ellington led his orchestra at the Cotton Club. But at that club, Black musicians performed for white-only audiences. Even at the center of Black culture, segregation was present.
The Harlem Renaissance showed the nation the talent and depth of Black *culture*. It gave African Americans a new sense of pride. It also shaped American literature and music for generations.

words.d: a flowering of African American writing, art and music centered in Harlem in the 1920s
the shared ways of life, beliefs, arts and customs of a group

look.title: Langston Hughes, “The Negro Speaks of Rivers”
look.text: I've known rivers: / I've known rivers ancient as the world and older than the flow of human blood in human veins. / My soul has grown deep like the rivers.
look.cite: Langston Hughes, poem published in The Crisis, 1921
look.prompt: What does the speaker mean by a soul that has “grown deep like the rivers”? What feeling about Black history does the poem express?

check.q: What was the Harlem Renaissance?
choices: A flowering of Black writing, art and music in the 1920s
check.why: Centered in Harlem, it celebrated African American life and culture.

check.q: Which writer was known for poems in the rhythms of jazz and blues?
check.why: Langston Hughes wrote poems shaped by jazz and blues about ordinary Black lives.

check.q: What does the Cotton Club show about the Harlem Renaissance?
choices: Segregation continued even at the center of Black culture
Only white musicians played in Harlem
Jazz was banned in New York
check.why: Black stars performed there, but the audiences were white only.

lessons.title: Marcus Garvey and Black Pride
lessons.mainIdea: Marcus Garvey built a mass movement that urged Black people around the world to take pride in their African heritage and build their own economic power.
reading: Marcus Garvey was born in Jamaica. In 1914 he founded the Universal Negro Improvement Association, or UNIA. In 1916 he moved to New York, and his movement grew quickly in Harlem and other cities.

Garvey told Black people to be proud of their African roots. He urged them to start their own businesses and depend on each other. He believed Black people would never be treated fairly in white-run nations. He called for building a strong independent nation in Africa. His followers marched in uniforms and read his newspaper.

Garvey started a shipping company called the Black Star Line. It was meant to carry goods and people between the Americas and Africa. But the company was badly run. It bought old, worn-out ships and lost a great deal of money that followers had invested.

Garvey had critics, including W.E.B. Du Bois of the NAACP. They disagreed with his plan to leave America and with how he ran his businesses. In 1923, Garvey was convicted of mail fraud. He was deported to Jamaica in 1927. His message of *Black pride* inspired later leaders.

words.d: the traditions and history passed down from earlier generations
a feeling of respect and pride in Black identity, history and culture

look.title: Two Paths
look.text: W.E.B. Du Bois wanted Black Americans to win full equal rights inside the United States through courts, protest and education. Marcus Garvey believed Black people should build their own businesses and a strong nation of their own in Africa.
look.prompt: What were the strengths and weaknesses of each approach? Which do you find more convincing, and why?

check.q: What organization did Marcus Garvey found?
check.why: Garvey founded the UNIA in 1914.

check.q: What was Garvey's main message?
choices: Black people should move to the rural South
Black people should take pride in their African heritage and build their own economic power
check.why: Garvey preached Black pride, self-reliance and building a strong nation in Africa.

check.q: Why did W.E.B. Du Bois criticize Garvey?
choices: He disagreed with Garvey's plan to leave America and how Garvey ran his businesses
He thought Garvey was too quiet
He wanted Garvey to join the Klan
check.why: Du Bois favored fighting for equal rights in the U.S. and questioned Garvey's leadership.

review.q: What made cars cheap enough for many families by the 1920s?

choices: It was only used by the army

choices: They all wrote for the Harlem Renaissance
