chapters.title: The Great Depression
chapters.bigQuestion: What should the government do when millions of ordinary people fall on hard times?

story.title: One Family Gets By
story.kicker: The Kowalski family is imaginary, but everything that happens to them happened to millions of real American families.
paragraphs: Picture a family in Chicago in 1929. Stan Kowalski works in a steel mill. His wife, Helen, keeps house and raises their three children. They rent a small flat. They have a radio, bought on credit, and a little savings in the neighborhood bank. They are not rich, but they feel secure. Then, in the fall, the stock market crashes.

At first, little changes for the Kowalskis. They own no stocks. But over the next year, orders for steel fall. Stan's hours are cut to three days a week. In 1931, the mill lays him off. That same year, their bank runs out of money and closes its doors. The family's savings are gone. There is no government insurance to pay them back.

Stan walks the city every day looking for work. So do thousands of other men. Helen takes in sewing and washing from neighbors who can still pay. The children pick up lumps of coal that fall from trains, to heat the flat. They eat a lot of bread and soup. Some days Stan stands in a long line at a soup kitchen. Even the gangster Al Capone opened one in Chicago, hoping to improve his image.

They fall behind on rent. The radio goes back to the store. Helen's brother loses his house and moves in with them, so now eight people share four rooms. The children see neighbors evicted, their furniture piled on the sidewalk. Stan feels ashamed that he cannot support his family, though the problem is far bigger than him.

In 1933, a new president takes office. That spring, the oldest son, Joe, joins the Civilian Conservation Corps. He plants trees in a forest far away and earns $30 a month. He is required to send $25 of it home. In 1935, Stan gets a job with the Works Progress Administration, building a new school. The pay is low, but it is steady. Like millions of families, the Kowalskis make it through by working hard, sharing what they have and getting help.
story.think: What helped the Kowalski family survive? Which help came from family and neighbors, and which came from the government?

lessons.title: Cracks Under the Boom
lessons.mainIdea: Behind the prosperity of the 1920s were serious weaknesses: struggling farmers, unequal wealth, too much debt and risky stock buying.
reading: The 1920s looked like good times. But the economy had hidden cracks. Farmers were one. During the war, they had grown extra crops for Europe. After the war, prices fell. Many farmers could not pay their debts and lost their land, years before the crash.

Wealth was also very unequal. A small group of rich families earned a large share of the nation's income. Most workers' pay rose slowly. Factories made more goods than ordinary people could afford to buy. This is called *overproduction*.
Many families bought cars, radios and furniture on credit. When they had borrowed as much as they could, they stopped buying. Then stores sold less, and factories had to slow down and cut workers.

The stock market was a big risk too. A *stock* is a small share of ownership in a company. In the late 1920s, stock prices rose fast. Many people bought stocks *on margin*. That meant they paid only a small part of the price and borrowed the rest. They believed prices would keep rising forever. If prices fell, they would owe money they did not have.

words.d: making more goods than people are able to buy
a share of ownership in a company that can be bought and sold
buying stock with a small amount of your own money and the rest borrowed

look.title: Borrowing on a Hunch
look.text: Imagine you buy a $100 stock but pay only $10. You borrow the other $90. If the stock rises to $150, you sell, pay back the $90 and have $60. You have made $50 from $10. But what if the stock falls to $50?
look.prompt: What happens to you if the stock falls to $50 and the lender wants the $90 back? Why was this so dangerous for the whole country?

check.q: Which group struggled even during the good times of the 1920s?
check.why: Crop prices fell after the war, and many farmers lost their land in the 1920s.

check.q: What does buying stock on margin mean?
choices: Selling stock you do not own
Paying a small part of the price and borrowing the rest
check.why: Margin buyers borrowed most of the money, so a price drop could wipe them out.

check.q: What is overproduction?
choices: Making more goods than people can afford to buy
check.why: When factories make more than people can buy, sales fall and factories cut jobs.

lessons.title: Black Tuesday
lessons.mainIdea: In October 1929, the stock market crashed, wiping out fortunes and shaking Americans' confidence.
reading: In September 1929, stock prices reached a record high. Then they began to slip. On Thursday, October 24, panicked owners rushed to sell. Prices dropped sharply. Bankers bought stocks to calm the market, and it steadied for a moment.

On Tuesday, October 29, 1929, the market collapsed. So many people wanted to sell that there were few buyers. More than 16 million shares were traded in one day, a record that stood for decades. This day became known as *Black Tuesday*.

People who had bought on margin were ruined. Lenders demanded their money back. Banks that had loaned money for stocks, or bought stocks themselves, lost huge sums. Some wealthy families lost almost everything in a few days.
The crash alone did not cause the *Great Depression*. But it helped start a downward spiral. Frightened people and businesses stopped spending. Stock prices kept sliding for almost three years.

words.d: October 29, 1929, the worst day of the stock market crash
the severe worldwide economic crisis that lasted from 1929 through the 1930s
sudden fear that makes many people act quickly without thinking

look.title: The Dow Jones Stock Average
look.cite: Dow Jones Industrial Average, closing values, rounded
look.prompt: About what share of its value did the stock average lose from 1929 to 1932? How long did it take to climb back?

check.q: What happened on Black Tuesday?
check.why: On October 29, 1929, stock prices fell sharply as millions of shares were sold.

check.q: Why were people who bought on margin ruined by the crash?
choices: They had no stocks to lose
They owed borrowed money that their falling stocks could not cover
They had paid for their stocks in cash
check.why: When prices fell, lenders demanded repayment that margin buyers could not afford.

check.q: Which statement about the crash is most accurate?
choices: It was the only cause of the Depression
It had no effect on the economy
It helped start the Depression but was not its only cause
check.why: Deeper weaknesses combined with the crash to cause the Depression.

lessons.title: Banks Fail, Jobs Vanish
lessons.mainIdea: Thousands of banks failed and about one in four workers lost their jobs, spreading hardship across the country.
reading: When people heard a bank was in trouble, they rushed to take out their money. This is called a *bank run*. Banks do not keep all deposits as cash; they lend most of it out. So a run could force a bank to close. About 9,000 banks failed between 1930 and 1933. When a bank closed, its customers' savings were often simply gone.

As people and businesses stopped spending, factories cut workers. Workers with no pay bought even less. More factories closed. By 1933, about one in four workers had no job. This is called *unemployment*. Many others worked fewer hours for lower pay.

The trouble spread around the world. In 1930, Congress passed a high tariff, a tax on imported goods, to protect American businesses. Other countries raised their own tariffs in return. World trade shrank, and the Depression grew worse.

Hardship reached every group. African Americans and Mexican Americans were often the first fired. Farmers watched prices fall so low that crops were not worth harvesting. Families lost homes and farms.

words.d: when many customers rush to take their money out of a bank at the same time
being without a job while wanting and able to work
a tax on goods brought in from other countries

look.title: Unemployment Rate in the U.S.
look.cite: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics historical estimates, rounded
look.prompt: In which year was unemployment highest? What happened between 1937 and 1938?

check.q: What is a bank run?
choices: When many customers rush to take out their money at once
A loan to buy a house
check.why: In a run, so many people withdraw at once that the bank can run out of cash.

check.q: About how many workers had no job by 1933?
check.why: Unemployment reached about 25 percent in 1933.

check.q: How did the high tariff of 1930 make the Depression worse?
choices: It lowered prices on all goods
Other countries raised tariffs too, and world trade shrank
check.why: Tariffs on both sides cut trade, hurting businesses and farmers that sold abroad.

lessons.title: Hoover Tries to Respond
lessons.mainIdea: President Hoover took some steps to fight the Depression, but he opposed direct federal help to individuals, and many Americans blamed him.
reading: Herbert Hoover became president in March 1929, just months before the crash. He was a skilled engineer who had organized food aid for Europe during World War I. He believed in *rugged individualism*, the idea that people should succeed through their own effort.

Hoover thought the economy would recover on its own. He asked business leaders to keep wages up. He urged churches, charities and local governments to help the needy. He believed direct federal *relief*, government money or food given to people in need, would make people depend on government.

As things got worse, Hoover did more. He supported building projects like the dam on the Colorado River later named Hoover Dam. In 1932 he created the Reconstruction Finance Corporation. It loaned money to banks, railroads and big businesses, hoping the help would trickle down to workers.

But charities ran out of money. Local governments went broke. Many Americans felt Hoover cared more about banks than about hungry families. That was not entirely fair, but his name became linked to hard times.

words.d: the belief that people should succeed through their own effort without help from government
money, food or other help given to people in need

look.title: Who Should Help?
look.text: Hoover believed local communities and charities should care for the needy, as they always had. By 1932, one city's charity might have enough money for only a few weeks of help, while thousands of families were hungry.
look.prompt: What are good reasons for help to come from local communities? What are good reasons for help to come from the national government?

check.q: What did Hoover mean by rugged individualism?
choices: People should succeed through their own effort
check.why: Hoover believed in self-reliance and worried that federal relief would create dependence.

check.q: What did the Reconstruction Finance Corporation do?
choices: Loaned money to banks, railroads and big businesses
Gave cash directly to every family
check.why: The RFC made loans to large institutions, hoping help would reach workers.

check.q: Why did many Americans blame Hoover?
choices: He started the war in Europe
They felt he helped banks more than hungry families
check.why: His refusal of direct federal relief made many believe he did not care about ordinary people.

lessons.title: Hoovervilles and the Bonus Army
lessons.mainIdea: Homeless families built shacktowns called Hoovervilles, and the army's removal of protesting veterans in 1932 turned many Americans against Hoover.
reading: Many families who lost their homes built shacks from scrap wood, tin and cardboard. Groups of these shacks grew on empty land in many cities, including Chicago. People bitterly called them *Hoovervilles*. A newspaper used as a blanket was a “Hoover blanket.” Thousands of young people rode freight trains from town to town looking for work.

In 1932, thousands of World War I veterans marched to Washington, D.C. Congress had promised them a *bonus*, an extra payment, for their service. But it was not due until 1945. The veterans needed it now. They camped with their families near the Capitol. They were called the Bonus Army.

The Senate voted against paying the bonus early. Most veterans went home, but thousands stayed. In July 1932, Hoover ordered the army to clear them out. Soldiers led by General Douglas MacArthur used tear gas and set the camp on fire.

Americans were shocked to see the army turned against veterans. The event badly hurt Hoover as the election of 1932 approached. To many voters, it seemed to sum up a government that had lost touch with suffering people.

words.d: a camp of shacks built by homeless people during the Depression
an extra payment; World War I veterans were promised one for their service
a person who has served in the military

look.title: A Protest in the Capital
look.text: The veterans of the Bonus Army had fought for their country. Now they were jobless and camped in the capital with their families. Their message was simple: we need the money we were promised, and we need it now.
look.prompt: The Constitution protects the right to peacefully ask the government for help. Should the government have handled the Bonus Army differently? How?

check.q: What were Hoovervilles?
choices: New towns built by the government
Camps of shacks built by homeless people
check.why: People named the shacktowns after the president they blamed.

check.q: What did the Bonus Army want?
choices: Early payment of a bonus promised to World War I veterans
check.why: Veterans wanted the bonus due in 1945 paid right away.

check.q: How did the Bonus Army affect Hoover?
choices: The army's attack on the veterans' camp badly hurt his popularity
It led him to pay the bonus early
It had no effect on the election
check.why: Images of soldiers driving out veterans turned many voters against Hoover.

lessons.title: The Dust Bowl
lessons.mainIdea: Drought and poor farming methods turned the southern Great Plains into a Dust Bowl, driving hundreds of thousands of people west.
reading: For years, farmers on the southern Great Plains plowed up the deep-rooted prairie grass to plant wheat. The grass had held the soil in place. In the early 1930s, a long *drought*, a time with little rain, struck the region.

With no grass and no rain, the dry soil blew away. Huge dust storms rolled across Oklahoma, Texas, Kansas, Colorado and New Mexico. The area became known as the *Dust Bowl*. On April 14, 1935, called Black Sunday, a giant storm turned day into night. People stuffed wet rags around windows. Dust got into food, beds and lungs.

Crops died and farms failed. Hundreds of thousands of people left. Many headed west to California, hoping to pick crops. Because many came from Oklahoma, they were all called “Okies,” often as an insult. In California, they found low pay, crowded camps and people who did not want them.

Photographer Dorothea Lange took pictures of *migrant* families for the government. Her pictures helped Americans understand the suffering. The government taught farmers to plant trees as windbreaks and to plow in ways that saved the soil.

words.d: a long period with little or no rain
the southern Great Plains region struck by drought and dust storms in the 1930s
a person who moves from place to place, often to find work

look.title: Human Choices, Natural Disaster
look.text: Droughts had hit the Plains before. But this time, millions of acres of prairie grass had been plowed under. Some scientists say the Dust Bowl was both a natural disaster and a human-made one.
look.prompt: What does it mean to say the Dust Bowl was partly human-made? What lesson might it hold for how we use land today?

check.q: What helped cause the Dust Bowl?
choices: Drought plus the plowing up of prairie grass
check.why: Without grass roots to hold the soil, drought let the wind blow it away.

check.q: Where did many Dust Bowl migrants go?
check.why: Many headed west to California hoping to find farm work.

check.q: How did Dorothea Lange's photographs help?
choices: They showed Americans the suffering of migrant families
check.why: Her pictures made the hardship of migrants real to people across the country.

lessons.title: Roosevelt Takes Charge
lessons.mainIdea: Franklin D. Roosevelt won the 1932 election by promising bold action, and he moved fast to restore Americans' confidence.
reading: In 1932, Democrat Franklin D. Roosevelt, the governor of New York, ran against Hoover. He promised “a new deal for the American people.” Roosevelt, often called FDR, came from a wealthy family. At age 39, he had been struck by polio and could no longer walk without help. Many said the illness made him more understanding of people who were suffering.

Roosevelt won in a landslide. When he took office on March 4, 1933, banks in many states had closed. Millions of people were out of work and frightened. In his first speech as president, he spoke directly to Americans' fear.

Two days later, Roosevelt closed all the nation's banks for a “bank holiday.” Congress quickly passed the Emergency Banking Act to inspect the banks. Only healthy banks would be allowed to reopen. When they did, people put money back in instead of rushing to take it out.

Roosevelt believed in trying new ideas and dropping those that failed. His programs became known as the *New Deal*. They aimed at three goals: *relief* for people in need, recovery for the economy, and reform to prevent another depression.

words.d: President Franklin Roosevelt's programs to fight the Great Depression
money, food or other help given to people in need
an election won by a very large number of votes

look.title: Roosevelt's First Inaugural Address
look.text: So, first of all, let me assert my firm belief that the only thing we have to fear is fear itself—nameless, unreasoning, unjustified terror which paralyzes needed efforts to convert retreat into advance.
look.cite: President Franklin D. Roosevelt, first inaugural address, March 4, 1933
look.prompt: Why would fear itself make the Depression worse? Think about bank runs and spending.

check.q: What were the three goals of the New Deal?
check.why: The New Deal aimed to help people now, rebuild the economy and prevent future crises.

check.q: Why did Roosevelt declare a bank holiday?
choices: To stop bank runs and reopen only healthy banks
check.why: Closing and inspecting the banks helped restore trust so people stopped withdrawing money.

check.q: In his first inaugural address, what did Roosevelt say Americans had to fear?
check.why: He said panic and fear were stopping the actions needed for recovery.

lessons.title: The First Hundred Days
lessons.mainIdea: In his first hundred days, Roosevelt and Congress created programs that protected savings, put young people to work and brought power to rural areas.
reading: Roosevelt's first months were a whirlwind. In about a hundred days, Congress passed more than a dozen major laws. On the radio, Roosevelt explained his plans in calm, simple talks from the White House. These became known as *fireside chats*.

The Banking Act of 1933 created the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, or FDIC. It insured people's bank savings. If a bank failed, the government would pay depositors back. The FDIC still protects savings today.

The Civilian Conservation Corps, or CCC, hired young men to plant trees, fight fires and build trails in parks. Over its life, about 3 million young men served. The Tennessee Valley Authority, or TVA, built dams in one of the poorest parts of the South. The dams controlled floods and made electricity.

Other programs tried to raise crop prices by paying farmers to grow less. Another tried to set fair rules for wages and prices in industry. Some worked better than others. Together, these programs brought the government into Americans' lives as never before.

words.d: one of Roosevelt's radio talks explaining his plans to the American people
the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, which insures people's bank savings
the careful protection of forests, soil, water and other natural resources

look.title: The First Fireside Chat
look.text: I can assure you that it is safer to keep your money in a reopened bank than under the mattress.
look.cite: President Franklin D. Roosevelt, fireside chat on banking, March 12, 1933
look.prompt: What was Roosevelt trying to get listeners to do? Why was speaking on the radio a smart way to do it?

check.q: What does the FDIC do?
choices: Hires young men to plant trees
check.why: The FDIC pays depositors back if an insured bank fails.

check.q: What kind of work did the Civilian Conservation Corps do?
choices: Planting trees, fighting fires and building park trails
check.why: The CCC put young men to work on conservation projects.

check.q: Why were the fireside chats important?
choices: They explained plans simply and helped build trust
check.why: Roosevelt used radio to speak directly and calmly to millions of Americans.

lessons.title: A Second Wave of Reform
lessons.mainIdea: The Second New Deal created jobs, Social Security and stronger rights for workers, changes that still shape American life.
reading: By 1935, the economy was better but still weak. Millions of people still had no jobs. Critics on all sides were growing louder. Roosevelt launched a new wave of programs, often called the Second New Deal.

The Works Progress Administration, or WPA, hired millions of jobless people. Over its life, about 8.5 million people worked for it. They built roads, bridges, schools, parks and airports. The WPA also hired artists to paint murals, writers to record local history and actors to put on plays.

The *Social Security* Act of 1935 created a system of payments for retired older workers. It also set up help for unemployed workers and some families with children. Workers and employers paid into the system from each paycheck.

Workers gained new rights. The Wagner Act of 1935 protected workers' right to form *labor unions* and bargain together for better pay. Union membership grew fast. In 1938, the Fair Labor Standards Act set the first national *minimum wage* and limited most child labor.

words.d: a government program that pays money to retired and disabled people, paid for by workers and employers
a group of workers who join together to seek better pay and working conditions
the lowest hourly pay an employer is allowed to pay by law

look.title: Signing Social Security
look.text: We can never insure one hundred percent of the population against one hundred percent of the hazards and vicissitudes of life, but we have tried to frame a law which will give some measure of protection to the average citizen and to his family against the loss of a job and against poverty-ridden old age.
look.cite: President Franklin D. Roosevelt, statement on signing the Social Security Act, August 14, 1935
look.prompt: Vicissitudes means ups and downs. What two dangers did Roosevelt want Social Security to protect against?

check.q: What did the WPA do?
choices: Hired millions to build roads, schools and parks and to make art
check.why: The WPA gave jobs to millions on public works and arts projects.

check.q: What did the Social Security Act create?
choices: Payments for retired older workers and help for the unemployed
check.why: Social Security set up retirement payments and unemployment help.

check.q: How did the Wagner Act help workers?
choices: It protected their right to form unions
check.why: The Wagner Act protected unions and bargaining together for better pay.

sections.title: Who Was Helped and Who Was Not

lessons.title: Women Who Led
lessons.mainIdea: Eleanor Roosevelt, Frances Perkins and Mary McLeod Bethune pushed the New Deal to help more people.
reading: Eleanor Roosevelt changed the role of First Lady. Because her husband could not easily travel, she crossed the country for him. She visited coal mines, farms and city slums. She wrote a newspaper column and held press conferences for women reporters. She spoke up for the poor, for women and for African Americans.

In 1939, a group refused to let Black singer Marian Anderson perform in its hall in Washington. Eleanor Roosevelt quit the group in protest. She helped arrange for Anderson to sing outdoors at the Lincoln Memorial. About 75,000 people came to hear her.

Frances Perkins became Secretary of Labor in 1933. She was the first woman in a president's *cabinet*, his group of top advisers. She played a key role in creating Social Security and the minimum wage.

Mary McLeod Bethune, an educator who had started a school in Florida that grew into a college, led a New Deal youth program's work with Black young people. She also led a group of Black officials who advised the president. Newspapers called it the Black Cabinet. She pushed the government to include African Americans in its programs.

words.d: the title for the wife of the president
the group of top advisers who lead government departments for the president

look.title: Eyes and Ears
look.text: Franklin Roosevelt sometimes asked Eleanor what she had seen on her travels. She told him about families without running water, schools without books and Black workers turned away from New Deal jobs.
look.prompt: Why is it important for leaders to hear directly from people who are struggling? How can leaders today do that?

check.q: Who was the first woman to serve in a president's cabinet?
check.why: Frances Perkins became Secretary of Labor in 1933.

check.q: What did Eleanor Roosevelt do when Marian Anderson was refused a concert hall?
choices: She quit the group in protest and helped arrange a concert at the Lincoln Memorial
She asked Congress to ban the concert
check.why: Her protest helped lead to Anderson's famous outdoor concert in 1939.

check.q: What was the Black Cabinet?
choices: A room in the White House
A group of Black business owners in Chicago
A New Deal program for farmers
A group of Black officials who advised the president
check.why: Mary McLeod Bethune led this group of advisers on issues facing African Americans.

lessons.title: Uneven Help
lessons.mainIdea: The New Deal helped many people, but African Americans, Mexican Americans and Native Americans often received less help or faced unfair treatment.
reading: African Americans were often “last hired, first fired” during the Depression. Some New Deal programs helped them, and the CCC and WPA hired many Black workers. But in the South, local officials often ran programs unfairly. Social Security at first did not cover farmworkers or household workers. Many Black workers held exactly those jobs. Farm programs that paid owners to plant less also pushed many Black *sharecroppers* off the land.
Even so, many African Americans felt Roosevelt's government cared more than earlier ones had. Many Black voters, who had long voted Republican, switched to the Democratic Party in the 1930s.

Mexican Americans faced a harsh campaign. As jobs disappeared, local and state officials pressured people of Mexican descent to leave the country. This was called *repatriation*. Hundreds of thousands left or were forced out. Many were U.S. citizens, including children born in the United States.

Native Americans saw a change in policy. The Indian Reorganization Act of 1934 ended the breaking up of tribal land into small plots. It encouraged tribes to form their own governments. Some nations welcomed it. Others felt it forced outside ideas of government on them.

words.d: a farmer who works land owned by someone else and pays with part of the crop
sending people back to the country they or their families came from

look.title: Citizens Sent Away
look.text: Imagine a ten-year-old girl born in Los Angeles in 1921. Her parents came from Mexico. In 1932, her family is pressured to leave. She speaks English, loves her school and has never seen Mexico. Now she must start over there.
look.prompt: What rights did this girl have as a U.S. citizen? Why do you think those rights were ignored?

check.q: Why did early Social Security leave out many Black workers?
choices: It did not cover farmworkers and household workers
It only covered people in the South
check.why: Many African Americans worked in farm and household jobs, which were not covered at first.

check.q: What was Mexican repatriation?
choices: A program that gave Mexican Americans jobs
Pressure and force that made hundreds of thousands of people of Mexican descent leave the U.S.
A new law allowing more immigrants
check.why: During the Depression, many people of Mexican descent, including U.S. citizens, were pushed out.

check.q: What did the Indian Reorganization Act of 1934 do?
choices: Ended the breaking up of tribal land and encouraged tribal governments
check.why: The law reversed the policy of dividing tribal land and supported tribal self-government.

lessons.title: Critics and Legacy
lessons.mainIdea: Critics said the New Deal did too much or too little, but many of its programs lasted, and full recovery came only with World War II.
reading: Not everyone liked the New Deal. Some business leaders and conservatives said it gave government too much power and spent too much money. They warned that it would make people depend on government and hurt freedom.

Others said Roosevelt did too little. Senator Huey Long of Louisiana wanted to take money from the rich and give every family a basic income. A radio priest, Father Charles Coughlin, attacked Roosevelt to millions of listeners. Dr. Francis Townsend proposed large monthly payments to older Americans.

The Supreme Court struck down some New Deal laws. In 1937, Roosevelt proposed adding up to six new justices to the Court. Critics said he was trying to “pack” the Court to get his way. Even many Democrats opposed the plan, and it failed. That same year, spending cuts helped cause a new downturn.

The New Deal did not end the Depression. Unemployment stayed high until huge spending for World War II created millions of jobs. But the New Deal changed what Americans expected of government. Social Security, the FDIC, the minimum wage and workers' rights to form unions are still part of American life. People still debate how big the government's role should be.

words.d: a person who prefers to keep traditions and limit government's role
Roosevelt's failed 1937 plan to add justices to the Supreme Court
something handed down from the past that still has effects

look.title: Roosevelt's Second Inaugural Address
look.text: I see one-third of a nation ill-housed, ill-clad, ill-nourished.
look.cite: President Franklin D. Roosevelt, second inaugural address, January 20, 1937
look.prompt: Four years into the New Deal, what problem is Roosevelt admitting? How might a supporter and a critic each respond?

check.q: Why did some critics oppose the New Deal?
choices: They said it banned all business
They wanted to end the Constitution
They said it gave government too much power and spent too much
check.why: Conservatives and many business leaders worried about government size, spending and freedom.

check.q: What was Roosevelt's court-packing plan?
choices: A plan to add justices to the Supreme Court
A plan to build new courthouses
A plan to end the Supreme Court
check.why: Roosevelt proposed adding up to six justices, but the plan failed.

check.q: What finally brought full recovery from the Depression?
choices: Huge spending and jobs for World War II
check.why: Wartime production created millions of jobs and ended high unemployment.

review.q: Which was a weakness in the economy of the 1920s?
choices: Many people bought stocks with borrowed money
review.why: Buying on margin made the market fragile, and a drop could ruin many people.

review.q: Why did thousands of banks fail in the early 1930s?
choices: The government closed them all forever
Banks were banned by the Constitution
Bank runs and bad loans drained their money
review.why: When many people withdrew at once, and loans went unpaid, banks ran out of cash.

review.q: How did Hoover's view differ from Roosevelt's?
choices: Hoover opposed direct federal relief, while Roosevelt used the government to help people directly
Hoover wanted more government programs than Roosevelt
Roosevelt wanted no help for banks
review.why: Hoover relied on charity and loans to business; Roosevelt created large federal relief programs.

review.q: What caused people to leave the Dust Bowl?
choices: Drought and dust storms destroyed their farms
review.why: Crops failed as the soil blew away, so many families moved west.

review.q: Which New Deal program still protects bank savings today?
review.why: The FDIC insures deposits so savers get their money back if a bank fails.

review.q: What did Social Security create?
choices: Payments for retired workers, paid for by workers and employers
review.why: Social Security set up retirement payments funded from paychecks.

review.q: Which group was pressured to leave the country during the Depression, even when they were U.S. citizens?
review.why: Repatriation campaigns pushed out hundreds of thousands of people of Mexican descent.

review.q: What is one lasting legacy of the New Deal?
choices: Americans expect the government to help in hard economic times
The end of the Supreme Court
review.why: Programs like Social Security and the FDIC changed what people expect government to do.

chapters.title: World War II
chapters.bigQuestion: How did fighting a war for freedom around the world test America's promise of freedom at home?

story.title: Only What You Could Carry
story.kicker: In 1942, the U.S. government forced about 120,000 people of Japanese ancestry from their homes, though most were American citizens.
paragraphs: On December 7, 1941, Japan attacked the U.S. Navy at Pearl Harbor in Hawaii. At that time, about 127,000 people of Japanese ancestry lived on the U.S. mainland, most of them on the West Coast. The older generation, called Issei, had been born in Japan. U.S. law did not allow them to become citizens. Their children, called Nisei, had been born in the United States. They were American citizens.

After Pearl Harbor, fear spread fast. Rumors said Japanese Americans might help Japan invade. There was no evidence of this, but old prejudice made the rumors easy to believe. On February 19, 1942, President Franklin Roosevelt signed Executive Order 9066. It let the military remove “any or all persons” from areas it chose. The order did not name any group, but it was used against Japanese Americans.

Army notices went up on telephone poles. Families had only days to get ready. They could bring only what they could carry. Many had to sell homes, farms, stores and fishing boats for a small part of what they were worth. Some lost everything. Families were given numbers and put on buses and trains, not knowing where they were going.

First they were held in temporary centers. Some were racetracks, where families slept in horse stalls. Then they were sent to ten camps in lonely places, such as Manzanar in the California desert and Heart Mountain in Wyoming. The camps had barbed wire fences and guard towers. Families lived in single rooms in long wooden barracks. Dust blew through the cracks. About two-thirds of the people held there were U.S. citizens.

People tried to make normal lives. They started schools, newspapers, gardens and baseball teams. Many older people used a Japanese saying, shikata ga nai: it cannot be helped. Thousands of young Nisei men joined the U.S. Army, even while their families stayed behind barbed wire. Others refused to be drafted until their families' rights were restored. When the camps closed in 1945 and 1946, many families had no homes to go back to. Thousands started over in cities like Chicago.
story.think: Most of the people sent to the camps were American citizens. What rights did the government take from them, and why do you think so many Americans went along with it?

lessons.title: Dictators on the March
lessons.mainIdea: In the 1920s and 1930s, dictators in Italy, Germany, the Soviet Union and Japan's military leaders built aggressive states that invaded their neighbors.
reading: The Great War and the Great Depression left many people angry and afraid. In several countries, they turned to *dictators*, rulers with total power. In Italy, Benito Mussolini took power in 1922. He started *fascism*, a system that puts the nation above the individual and crushes all opposition. In the Soviet Union, Joseph Stalin ruled through terror. Millions of his own people died because of his harsh policies.

In Germany, Adolf Hitler led the Nazi Party. He blamed Germany's problems on the Treaty of Versailles and on Jewish people. He promised to make Germany powerful again. Hitler became chancellor, or head of government, in 1933. He soon ended democracy and began building up the army. In Japan, military leaders gained control of the government. They wanted an empire in Asia to supply oil, rubber and other resources.

These nations began taking land. Japan seized Manchuria, in northern China, in 1931 and invaded the rest of China in 1937. Italy invaded Ethiopia in 1935. Germany took over Austria in 1938. Then Hitler demanded part of Czechoslovakia. Britain and France agreed at a meeting in Munich, hoping to avoid war. Giving in to an aggressor's demands to keep peace is called *appeasement*.

Appeasement failed. In 1939, Hitler took the rest of Czechoslovakia. On September 1, 1939, Germany invaded Poland. Britain and France declared war on Germany. World War II had begun. By June 1940, Germany had conquered France. Britain fought on almost alone. Germany, Italy and Japan became allies called the *Axis Powers*.

words.d: a ruler who has total power over a country
a system of government that puts the nation above individuals, is led by a dictator and crushes opposition
giving in to an aggressor's demands in order to keep peace
in World War II, Germany, Italy, Japan and their allies

look.title: Would Giving In Work?
look.text: In 1938, many people in Britain and France remembered the millions killed in the Great War. They did not want another war. Their leaders thought that if Hitler got part of Czechoslovakia, he would be satisfied. Six months later, he took the rest of the country.
look.prompt: Why did appeasement seem reasonable to many people at the time? What lesson did leaders take from its failure?

check.q: What is appeasement?
choices: Giving in to an aggressor's demands to keep peace
check.why: Britain and France practiced appeasement when they let Hitler take part of Czechoslovakia.

check.q: What event began World War II in Europe?
check.why: Britain and France declared war after Germany invaded Poland on September 1, 1939.

check.q: Whom did Hitler blame for Germany's problems?
choices: The Treaty of Versailles and Jewish people
check.why: Hitler spread anger about the treaty and hatred of Jewish people to gain power.

lessons.title: From Neutral to Arsenal
lessons.mainIdea: Americans wanted to stay out of the war, but Roosevelt found ways to send help to Britain and other nations fighting the Axis.
reading: Many Americans remembered World War I and wanted no part of another European war. People who want their nation to stay out of other countries' affairs are called *isolationists*. In the mid-1930s, Congress passed Neutrality Acts that limited selling weapons to nations at war.

After war began in 1939, Roosevelt believed the United States could not be safe if Hitler won. Congress agreed to let Britain and France buy weapons if they paid cash and carried the goods in their own ships. In 1940, the nation started its first peacetime draft.

The America First Committee, based in Chicago, argued hard against getting involved. Its best-known speaker was the pilot Charles Lindbergh. Other Americans said the country had to help Britain survive.

In January 1941, Roosevelt spoke of Four Freedoms that all people deserved. In March, Congress passed the *Lend-Lease* Act. It let the United States lend or lease weapons and supplies to Britain, and later to the Soviet Union and others. Roosevelt said America would be the “arsenal of democracy,” a storehouse of weapons for nations fighting the Axis.

words.d: a person who wants their nation to stay out of other countries' affairs and wars
the 1941 program that let the U.S. lend or lease war supplies to nations fighting the Axis
a place where weapons are made or stored

look.title: The Four Freedoms
look.text: …we look forward to a world founded upon four essential human freedoms. The first is freedom of speech and expression… The second is freedom of every person to worship God in his own way… The third is freedom from want… The fourth is freedom from fear…
look.cite: President Franklin D. Roosevelt, State of the Union address, January 6, 1941
look.prompt: Which of the Four Freedoms do you think matters most? Why would Roosevelt describe the war in terms of freedoms?

check.q: What is an isolationist?
choices: Someone who wants to conquer other lands
Someone who wants their nation to stay out of other countries' wars
A person who lives on an island
check.why: Isolationists, like the America First Committee, wanted the U.S. to stay out of the war.

check.q: What did the Lend-Lease Act do?
choices: Let the U.S. lend or lease war supplies to nations fighting the Axis
check.why: Lend-Lease sent weapons and supplies to Britain and later other Allies.

check.q: Which of these was one of Roosevelt's Four Freedoms?
check.why: Roosevelt named freedom of speech, of worship, from want and from fear.

lessons.title: Pearl Harbor
lessons.mainIdea: Japan's surprise attack on Pearl Harbor on December 7, 1941, brought the United States into World War II.
reading: Japan wanted to control East Asia and its resources. When Japan moved into French Indochina in 1941, the United States cut off sales of oil to Japan. Japan needed oil for its navy. Its leaders decided to strike the U.S. Pacific Fleet so America could not stop them.

Early on Sunday morning, December 7, 1941, Japanese planes attacked the naval base at Pearl Harbor, Hawaii. They sank or damaged eight battleships and destroyed many planes. More than 2,400 Americans were killed. The battleship Arizona exploded and sank with more than 1,100 sailors aboard. Luckily for the U.S., its aircraft carriers were at sea that day.

The next day, Roosevelt spoke to Congress. Congress quickly declared war on Japan. Only one member voted no: Jeannette Rankin, who had also voted against war in 1917. On December 11, Germany and Italy declared war on the United States.

The attack ended the debate over isolation. Americans were now united and angry. Millions rushed to join the military. The United States joined Britain, the Soviet Union, China and others as the *Allies*.

words.d: a U.S. naval base in Hawaii attacked by Japan on December 7, 1941
in World War II, the nations that fought the Axis, including the U.S., Britain, the Soviet Union and China
being famous for something shameful or evil

look.title: A Date Which Will Live in Infamy
look.text: Yesterday, December 7th, 1941—a date which will live in infamy—the United States of America was suddenly and deliberately attacked by naval and air forces of the Empire of Japan.
look.cite: President Franklin D. Roosevelt, address to Congress, December 8, 1941
look.prompt: Why did Roosevelt use the words “suddenly and deliberately”? How do they make the case for war?

check.q: Why did Japan attack Pearl Harbor?
choices: To cripple the U.S. Pacific Fleet so America could not stop Japan's expansion
Because the U.S. had invaded Japan
To win back land in Texas
check.why: Japan hoped a surprise blow would keep the U.S. from blocking its plans in Asia.

check.q: What happened the day after the attack?
choices: Germany made peace with the U.S.
check.why: After Roosevelt's speech on December 8, Congress declared war on Japan.

check.q: How did Pearl Harbor change public opinion?
choices: It made most Americans want to stay out of the war
It ended the debate over isolation and united Americans for war
check.why: The attack turned a divided country into one determined to fight.

lessons.title: Factories, Rations and Rosie
lessons.mainIdea: Americans at home turned factories into war plants, lived with rationing and filled millions of jobs, many of them women.
reading: Winning the war meant making huge amounts of weapons. The government told factories what to build. Car companies stopped making cars for families and built tanks, trucks, airplane engines and more. This shift to wartime production is called *mobilization*. Jobs appeared everywhere, and the Depression finally ended.

Illinois played a big part. Chicago plants built engines, radios and ships' parts. In the small town of Seneca, on the Illinois River, workers built landing ships for the Navy. Great Lakes Naval Training Station, north of Chicago, trained huge numbers of sailors.

Many goods were in short supply. The government used *rationing*, limiting how much of certain goods each family could buy. Families got ration books with stamps for sugar, coffee, meat, gas and tires. People planted victory gardens to grow their own vegetables. Children collected scrap metal and rubber. Families bought war bonds to lend money to the government.

With millions of men in uniform, millions of women took jobs in factories and shipyards. They welded, riveted and ran machines. The image of “Rosie the Riveter” became a symbol of these workers. Hundreds of thousands of women also joined the military in new women's branches. Most were pushed out of factory jobs when the men came home, but the war changed ideas about women's work.

words.d: getting a nation's people, factories and resources ready for war
limiting the amount of certain goods each person can buy
a loan from citizens to the government to help pay for a war

look.title: Americans on Active Military Duty
look.cite: U.S. Department of Defense, rounded
look.prompt: About how many times larger was the military in 1945 than in 1939? Who filled the jobs those millions of people left behind?

check.q: What is rationing?
choices: Limiting how much of certain goods each family can buy
check.why: Rationing used stamps to limit goods like sugar, meat and gas.

check.q: What did “Rosie the Riveter” stand for?
choices: Women who worked in war factories
check.why: Rosie was a symbol of the millions of women who took factory jobs during the war.

check.q: How did the war end the Great Depression?
choices: War production created millions of jobs
check.why: Mobilization put nearly everyone who wanted a job to work.

lessons.title: Fighting for Freedom Twice
lessons.mainIdea: African Americans, Native Americans and Mexican Americans served bravely while still facing discrimination at home.
reading: More than a million African Americans served in World War II, in a military that was still segregated. A Black newspaper called for a *Double V* campaign: victory over enemies abroad and victory over racism at home. In 1941, labor leader A. Philip Randolph planned a march on Washington to protest job discrimination. Roosevelt then signed an order banning discrimination in defense industries.
The *Tuskegee Airmen* were the first Black military pilots in U.S. history. They trained at Tuskegee, Alabama. Flying over Europe, they protected American bombers and earned a strong record.

Native Americans served in large numbers. About 400 Navajo Marines became *code talkers*. They used their own language to create a code for sending messages in the Pacific. The enemy never broke it. Code talkers from other nations, such as the Comanche, also served.

Hundreds of thousands of Mexican Americans served, and many earned high honors. At home, the Bracero Program brought Mexican workers to farms and railroads. But in 1943, in Los Angeles, groups of servicemen attacked young Mexican Americans in the Zoot Suit Riots. Chinese Americans also served, and in 1943 Congress repealed the Chinese Exclusion Act.

words.d: the campaign for victory over enemies abroad and over racism at home
the first African American military pilots, who trained at Tuskegee, Alabama
a Native American service member who used a Native language to send secret military messages

look.title: Two Victories
look.text: A Black soldier from Chicago might fight in Europe for freedom. When his train crossed into the South, he could be forced to sit in a separate car. In some places, German prisoners of war were allowed to eat in restaurants that refused to serve Black American soldiers.
look.prompt: Why did so many people facing discrimination still choose to serve? How might their service help the fight for equal rights after the war?

check.q: What was the Double V campaign?
choices: A plan to win two battles in one day
A program to sell war bonds
A code used by the Navy
A call for victory over enemies abroad and over racism at home
check.why: African Americans linked the fight against fascism with the fight against racism at home.

check.q: What did the Navajo code talkers do?
choices: Used their language to send secret messages the enemy never broke
Worked on farms in the Bracero Program
check.why: Their code, based on the Navajo language, kept Marine messages secret.

check.q: Who were the Tuskegee Airmen?
choices: The first African American military pilots
check.why: The Tuskegee Airmen trained in Alabama and flew missions over Europe.

lessons.title: Executive Order 9066
lessons.mainIdea: The forced removal of Japanese Americans was later judged a grave injustice, and in 1988 the U.S. government formally apologized.
reading: Under Executive Order 9066, about 120,000 people of Japanese ancestry were forced into camps. This is called *incarceration*, being locked up. No Japanese American was ever convicted of spying for Japan during the war. In Hawaii, where people of Japanese ancestry made up about a third of the population, there was no mass removal. German and Italian Americans were not removed as whole groups either.

Some people fought back in court. Fred Korematsu, a young welder in California, refused to leave his home. He was arrested. In 1944, in Korematsu v. United States, the Supreme Court ruled 6 to 3 that the removal was allowed because of wartime needs. Three justices disagreed, and one called it racism. The same day, in another case, the Court ruled that the government could not keep loyal citizens locked up. The camps began to close.

Thousands of Nisei men served in the U.S. Army. The 442nd Regimental Combat Team, made up mostly of Japanese Americans, fought in Italy and France. It became one of the most decorated units in American history.

Years later, Japanese Americans pushed for *redress*, making things right. In 1983, Korematsu's conviction was overturned. In 1988, President Ronald Reagan signed the Civil Liberties Act. It apologized and paid $20,000 to each surviving person who had been held.

words.d: being locked up or confined, as in a prison or camp
action taken to make up for a wrong
basic freedoms, like speech and fair treatment under the law, that government may not take away

look.title: Congress Looks Back
look.text: …these actions were carried out without adequate security reasons and without any acts of espionage or sabotage documented by the Commission, and were motivated largely by racial prejudice, wartime hysteria, and a failure of political leadership.
look.cite: Civil Liberties Act of 1988, passed by Congress and signed by President Ronald Reagan
look.prompt: Congress named three causes of the incarceration. Explain each one in your own words.

check.q: What did the Supreme Court decide in Korematsu v. United States in 1944?
choices: The camps were illegal and must close that day
Fred Korematsu should be given a medal
The removal was allowed because of wartime needs
Japanese Americans could not serve in the army
check.why: The Court ruled 6 to 3 against Korematsu, a decision now widely seen as wrong.

check.q: What did the Civil Liberties Act of 1988 do?
choices: Apologized and paid $20,000 to each surviving person who had been held
check.why: Congress and President Reagan formally apologized and paid redress.

check.q: Which fact shows that the incarceration was not based on real danger?
choices: No Japanese American was convicted of spying for Japan during the war
check.why: With no spying found, the removal rested on prejudice rather than evidence.

lessons.title: Turning the Tide
lessons.mainIdea: The Allies focused first on defeating Germany, winning key victories in the Atlantic, the Soviet Union, North Africa and Italy.
reading: The Allies agreed to defeat Germany first, since it was the strongest Axis power. In the Atlantic, German U-boats sank hundreds of ships carrying supplies. Over time, the Allies used radar, air patrols and warship escorts to win this battle.

In 1941, Hitler had invaded the Soviet Union. At first the Germans swept forward. But in the winter of 1942 to 1943, the Soviet army trapped and defeated a huge German army at Stalingrad. It was a major *turning point*. From then on, Germany was mostly retreating in the east. The Soviet people suffered enormous losses in the war.
In November 1942, American and British troops landed in North Africa. Americans lost their first big battle there, but they learned fast. By May 1943, the Axis armies in North Africa had surrendered.

Next, the Allies invaded Sicily and then Italy in 1943. Italian leaders removed Mussolini from power. But German troops fought on in Italy's mountains. The Allies freed Rome in June 1944. Meanwhile, Allied bombers struck German factories, railroads and cities.

words.d: an event after which things change in an important way
to move back or away from an enemy

look.title: Why Germany First?
look.text: After Pearl Harbor, many Americans wanted revenge on Japan. But Roosevelt and British leader Winston Churchill agreed to focus first on Germany. Germany had the strongest army and factories, and it threatened Britain and the Soviet Union directly.
look.prompt: Do you think “Germany first” was a wise strategy? What might have happened if the Allies had focused on Japan first?

check.q: Why was the Battle of Stalingrad a turning point?
choices: It was where the U.S. entered the war
After it, Germany was mostly retreating in the east
It ended the war in the Pacific
check.why: The Soviet victory at Stalingrad stopped Germany's advance in the east.

check.q: Where did American troops first fight Germany on land?
check.why: American and British troops landed in North Africa in November 1942.

check.q: What was the Allies' main strategy early in the war?
check.why: The Allies focused on Germany, the strongest Axis power.

lessons.title: D-Day and Victory
lessons.mainIdea: On D-Day, June 6, 1944, the Allies invaded France, and less than a year later, Germany surrendered.
reading: For years, the Soviet Union had asked Britain and the U.S. to open a second front in Western Europe. The Allies planned a huge invasion of Normandy, on the coast of France. General Dwight D. Eisenhower led it.

On June 6, 1944, called *D-Day*, about 156,000 Allied soldiers crossed the English Channel by ship and plane. Americans landed at beaches code-named Utah and Omaha. At Omaha Beach, the fighting was fierce, and many soldiers died. By nightfall, the Allies held the beaches. Soon they poured more troops into France.

In August 1944, Paris was freed. In December, Germany launched a surprise attack in Belgium. This was the Battle of the Bulge, the largest battle Americans fought in the war. The Allies held on and pushed into Germany from the west while Soviet troops pushed in from the east.

On April 12, 1945, President Roosevelt died. Vice President Harry S. Truman became president. On April 30, Hitler killed himself. Germany surrendered on May 8, 1945, called *V-E Day*, for Victory in Europe. Crowds celebrated in cities across America.

words.d: June 6, 1944, when Allied forces invaded Normandy, France
May 8, 1945, Victory in Europe Day, when Germany surrendered
an attack in which an army enters another country

look.title: Eisenhower's Message to the Troops
look.text: Soldiers, Sailors and Airmen of the Allied Expeditionary Force! You are about to embark upon the Great Crusade, toward which we have striven these many months. The eyes of the world are upon you.
look.cite: General Dwight D. Eisenhower, order of the day, June 6, 1944
look.prompt: How do you think soldiers felt reading this message just before the landing? Why would Eisenhower call it a crusade?

check.q: What happened on D-Day?
check.why: On June 6, 1944, Allied forces landed on the beaches of Normandy.

check.q: Who led the D-Day invasion?
check.why: Eisenhower commanded the Allied invasion of Normandy.

check.q: Why was opening a front in France so important?
choices: It ended the war with Japan
It gave the Allies more oil
It forced Germany to fight the Allies from the west while the Soviets attacked from the east
check.why: Squeezed between two fronts, Germany could not hold out.

lessons.title: The Holocaust
lessons.mainIdea: Nazi Germany and its collaborators murdered about six million Jews, along with millions of other people, in the Holocaust.
reading: The *Holocaust* was the planned, government-run persecution and murder of about six million Jewish men, women and children by Nazi Germany and its helpers, from 1933 to 1945. *Persecution* means cruel, unfair treatment of people because of who they are. The Nazis also persecuted and murdered millions of others, including Roma people, people with disabilities, Poles and Soviet prisoners of war. They imprisoned political opponents, gay men and Jehovah's Witnesses.

It began with hateful words and unfair laws. Hitler spread *antisemitism*, hatred of Jewish people. In 1935, new laws took away German Jews' citizenship. On November 9 and 10, 1938, Nazis attacked Jewish homes, shops and synagogues across Germany and Austria. This is called Kristallnacht, the Night of Broken Glass. About 30,000 Jewish men were sent to prison camps.

During the war, the Nazis forced Jews into crowded, walled-off city areas called ghettos. Killing squads murdered Jews in Eastern Europe. Then the Nazis built death camps, such as Auschwitz-Birkenau and Treblinka, where people were killed on a huge scale. About one and a half million of the victims were children. Anne Frank, a Jewish girl who kept a diary while hiding in Amsterdam, died in a camp in 1945 at age 15. Jews resisted, as in the Warsaw Ghetto uprising of 1943. Some non-Jews risked their lives to hide them.

Before the war, the U.S. kept strict immigration quotas and let in relatively few Jewish refugees. In 1939, the ship St. Louis, carrying more than 900 Jewish refugees, was turned away by Cuba and not allowed into the U.S. In 1944, Roosevelt created the War Refugee Board, which helped save many thousands. In 1945, American soldiers freed prisoners at camps like Buchenwald and Dachau. Survivors' stories, shared in places like the Illinois Holocaust Museum in Skokie, help the world remember.

words.d: the planned persecution and murder of about six million Jews by Nazi Germany and its helpers, 1933 to 1945
cruel, unfair treatment of people because of who they are or what they believe
hatred of or prejudice against Jewish people
a person who flees their home country to escape danger

look.title: An American General Bears Witness
look.text: What I saw at this camp is beyond words. I went there on purpose, so that if anyone in the future ever claims these crimes are only propaganda, I can give evidence as an eyewitness.
look.cite: General Dwight D. Eisenhower, letter to General George C. Marshall after visiting the Ohrdruf camp, April 1945 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Why did Eisenhower think it was important to see the camp himself? Why does bearing witness still matter today?

check.q: What was the Holocaust?
choices: A battle between Germany and the Soviet Union
A peace treaty that ended World War II
A program to rebuild Europe after the war
The planned persecution and murder of about six million Jews by Nazi Germany and its helpers
check.why: The Holocaust was the Nazis' planned murder of about six million Jews, along with millions of other victims.

check.q: How did the persecution of Jews in Germany begin?
choices: With hateful words and laws that took away their rights
With the attack on Pearl Harbor
check.why: Antisemitic speech and laws, like those taking away citizenship in 1935, came before the mass murder.

check.q: Why is the story of the ship St. Louis important?
choices: It carried the first American soldiers to Europe
It shows that refugees trying to escape were turned away, including by the U.S.
It brought Anne Frank to America
check.why: The St. Louis was refused entry, and it returned its Jewish passengers to Europe.

sections.title: Victory in the Pacific and the Peace

lessons.title: Island by Island
lessons.mainIdea: After early Japanese victories, the U.S. won at Midway and then fought island by island toward Japan.
reading: After Pearl Harbor, Japan won victory after victory. It captured the Philippines, where U.S. and Filipino troops surrendered in April 1942. Japanese soldiers forced the prisoners on a brutal march, and thousands died. It became known as the Bataan Death March.

In June 1942, the U.S. Navy won a huge victory at the Battle of *Midway*. American code breakers had learned Japan's plans. U.S. planes sank four Japanese aircraft carriers. Japan's navy never fully recovered. Midway was the turning point in the Pacific.

The Allies then used *island hopping*. Instead of attacking every Japanese-held island, they captured key ones and skipped others. Each captured island gave them airfields closer to Japan. The fighting was fierce. At Guadalcanal, Iwo Jima and Okinawa, Japanese soldiers fought almost to the last person.

Near the end of the war, some Japanese pilots crashed their planes on purpose into American ships. They were called kamikaze pilots. The high losses made American leaders fear that invading Japan itself would cost a great many lives.

lessons.title: The Atomic Bomb
lessons.mainIdea: The United States built atomic bombs in secret and dropped two on Japan in August 1945, and Japan surrendered soon after.
reading: Scientists warned Roosevelt that Germany might build a powerful new weapon from splitting atoms. The U.S. started a secret program called the *Manhattan Project*. On December 2, 1942, under the stands of a stadium at the University of Chicago, a team led by Enrico Fermi created the first controlled nuclear chain reaction. It proved an atomic bomb was possible.

In July 1945, scientists tested the first atomic bomb in the New Mexico desert. President Truman now had to decide whether to use it. Japan had refused to surrender. Military leaders expected an invasion of Japan to cost huge numbers of lives on both sides.

On August 6, 1945, a U.S. plane dropped an *atomic bomb* on the city of Hiroshima. On August 9, a second bomb destroyed much of Nagasaki. The Soviet Union also declared war on Japan. By the end of 1945, well over 100,000 people had died in the two cities, most of them civilians. Many survivors suffered from radiation sickness for years.

Japan announced its surrender on August 15, 1945. The formal surrender was signed on September 2. People still debate the decision. Supporters argue the bombs ended the war quickly and saved lives by avoiding an invasion. Critics argue Japan was close to defeat, and that killing so many civilians was wrong.

lessons.title: The Cost and the Peace
lessons.mainIdea: World War II was the deadliest war in history, and it left the United States a world superpower that helped create the United Nations.
reading: World War II was the deadliest war in human history. More than 60 million people died, most of them civilians. Cities across Europe and Asia lay in ruins. Millions of people had lost their homes. About 16 million Americans served in the military, and about 405,000 died.

After the war, the Allies put Nazi leaders on trial at Nuremberg, Germany, for *war crimes* and crimes against humanity. For the first time, leaders were held responsible before an international court for the murder of civilians. Japanese leaders were also tried.

Leaders wanted to stop another world war. In 1945, delegates from 50 nations met in San Francisco and signed a charter creating the *United Nations*. This time, unlike after World War I, the United States joined. The UN was set up to help settle disputes, protect human rights and help people in need.

The war changed the United States. It came out as a *superpower*, a nation with enormous military and economic strength. So did the Soviet Union, and the two soon became rivals. At home, veterans returned to a booming economy. The service of women and people of color would fuel new demands for equal rights.
